title: Accountants and auditors
rationale: Accounting is predominantly digital and rules-based, allowing AI to automate transaction classification, reconciliation, tax preparation, document review, anomaly detection, and portions of audit testing. Demand should expand moderately as lower costs make sophisticated accounting, compliance, risk analysis, and advisory services accessible to more small businesses, but statutory requirements and the finite number of entities limit expansion. The occupation will therefore restructure: fewer workers will perform routine preparation and testing, while greater emphasis shifts toward judgment, validation, client communication, regulatory accountability, and strategic advice.

title: Actors
rationale: Generative video, synthetic voices, digital likenesses, and automated dubbing directly threaten voiceover work, extras, and some screen roles while also changing auditions and production workflows. Live theater, interactive performances, celebrity appeal, and roles requiring authentic ensemble interaction remain comparatively resistant, keeping disruption below the highest levels. Cheaper production could generate more localized, personalized, and niche entertainment, but limited audience attention and production budgets constrain how much of that expansion will employ human actors. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around distinctive human performance, live work, and likeness management rather than disappear altogether.

title: Actuaries
rationale: Actuarial work is predominantly digital and analytical, including data preparation, statistical modeling, forecasting, policy testing, and report production—all tasks increasingly accelerated by AI. Demand may expand as new risks, data sources, and insurance products emerge, but regulation, certification requirements, market size, and the limited need for repeated formal risk assessments constrain how much additional output will be consumed. Human judgment, communication, model validation, and professional accountability remain important, but substantial productivity gains are likely to reduce staffing needs per portfolio, making replace the best fit.

title: Administrative services and facilities managers
rationale: AI will materially improve records management, compliance tracking, procurement, scheduling, energy analysis, reporting, and preventive-maintenance planning. However, supervising staff, inspecting facilities, coordinating contractors, handling emergencies, and bearing responsibility for safety and regulatory compliance still require substantial human judgment and real-world presence. Demand is relatively inelastic because organizations will not need proportionally more facilities or administrative oversight when management becomes cheaper, but the occupation remains resilient because disruption does not fully reach its physical and interpersonal core.

title: Adult basic and secondary education and ESL teachers
rationale: AI can already generate lessons, translate explanations, assess proficiency, provide conversational practice, and personalize exercises, materially changing much of teachers’ instructional and administrative work. Human teachers remain important for motivation, cultural sensitivity, classroom management, disability recognition, and connecting vulnerable learners with community resources. Demand is highly elastic because inexpensive, individualized instruction could reach many adults currently excluded by cost, scheduling, geography, or limited program capacity, so expanded access should absorb substantial productivity gains and make augmentation more likely than replacement.

title: Advertising sales agents
rationale: AI can automate prospect research, lead scoring, outreach, proposal generation, pricing, reporting, account administration, and much of digital ad placement. Human persuasion, negotiation, and relationship management remain important for complex or high-value accounts, but a large share of routine sales activity is directly exposed. Demand expansion is limited by advertisers’ budgets, finite consumer attention, and the growing use of self-service advertising platforms, so cheaper sales work will not produce a proportional increase in agents. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore points to replacement and significant headcount contraction.

title: Advertising, promotions, and marketing managers
rationale: AI can substantially automate market research, customer segmentation, campaign design, content generation, media placement, pricing analysis, and performance reporting. However, client relationships, cross-functional leadership, negotiation, accountability, and high-stakes strategic judgment remain human-centered. Lower campaign costs will enable more personalization, experimentation, and marketing by smaller firms, but the number of managerial positions remains partly tied to organizations, budgets, and team structures. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-enabled strategy and oversight rather than experience either wholesale replacement or proportionate headcount growth.

title: Aerospace engineering and operations technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can accelerate simulation, test-data analysis, anomaly detection, documentation, and predictive maintenance, materially changing the occupation’s cognitive tasks. However, technicians must still install instruments, build and maintain test facilities, calibrate physical equipment, troubleshoot hardware, and ensure safety in tightly controlled real-world environments. Cheaper testing and development could support more satellites, drones, and advanced aircraft, but capital costs, regulation, and manufacturing constraints limit demand expansion, so moderate disruption and elasticity make the occupation resilient.

title: Aerospace engineers
rationale: Much of aerospace engineering involves computer-based design, simulation, optimization, analysis, coding, and technical documentation, making AI materially useful across core workflows. However, physical testing, systems integration, safety certification, security requirements, and professional accountability limit full automation. Cheaper engineering could unlock more satellites, drones, design iterations, and specialized aerospace products, but capital costs, regulation, manufacturing capacity, and procurement cycles constrain demand expansion. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-assisted design and validation rather than experience either wholesale replacement or demand-driven expansion sufficient for augmentation.

title: Agricultural and food science technicians
rationale: AI will materially improve data analysis, anomaly detection, experimental documentation, report preparation, and interpretation of test results. However, much of the occupation still requires physical sample collection and preparation, equipment operation, sterile laboratory procedures, fieldwork, and judgment in variable farms and processing plants. Cheaper testing and analysis could support more quality control, product development, and agricultural research, but demand remains constrained by production volumes, research budgets, and regulatory testing requirements. The mixed physical-digital task profile keeps disruption moderate, so the occupation is resilient even as its analytical workflows become more automated.

title: Agricultural and food scientists
rationale: AI will substantially accelerate literature review, experimental design, genomic and sensor-data analysis, modeling, regulatory documentation, and technical writing. However, core work still requires laboratory experiments, field sampling, facility inspections, biological validation, and judgment in variable real-world environments. Cheaper research could unlock considerable demand for crop resilience, food safety, sustainable production, and new products, although physical testing cycles limit the expansion. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient, with scientists becoming more productive rather than broadly replaced.

title: Agricultural engineers
rationale: AI will materially improve computer-aided design, simulation, geospatial analysis, optimization, documentation, and diagnostics. However, agricultural engineering also requires site-specific investigation, physical testing, construction oversight, safety validation, regulatory accountability, and coordination in unpredictable farm environments. Cheaper engineering could expand precision agriculture, automation, environmental-control, and resource-efficiency projects, although farm capital constraints and the finite number of facilities limit demand growth. Because AI substantially assists but does not take over the occupation's field-based and accountable core, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Agricultural workers
rationale: Most core tasks involve physical labor, dexterity, machinery operation, and work with crops or animals in variable outdoor environments, placing them beyond the direct reach of current generative AI. AI-enabled precision agriculture, autonomous equipment, robotic harvesting, and livestock monitoring will automate selected tasks, but deployment costs and difficult real-world conditions will limit occupation-wide disruption over the next decade. Demand is highly inelastic because food consumption will not rise proportionally if agricultural labor becomes much cheaper, while land, water, and biological constraints further limit output expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient under the scoring framework, although conventional labor roles may gradually shift toward operating and servicing automated equipment.

title: Air traffic controllers
rationale: The work is predominantly digital, cognitive, and communications-based, making conflict detection, routing, clearances, monitoring, and handoffs increasingly amenable to AI-assisted automation. Safety-critical edge cases, regulatory requirements, and the need for accountable human judgment will slow full autonomy, but controllers may supervise substantially more traffic with automated support. Demand for controllers is tied mainly to flight volume rather than the cost of control services, so cheaper processing would generate little additional demand. High disruption combined with low elasticity therefore points to replacement pressure and gradual headcount contraction, even if humans remain in the loop.

title: Aircraft and avionics equipment mechanics and technicians
rationale: AI will improve fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, interpretation of technical manuals and flight data, parts identification, and recordkeeping. However, the core work still requires certified personnel to physically inspect, test, install, adjust, and repair safety-critical equipment in varied real-world settings. Demand is tied mainly to fleet size, aircraft utilization, and FAA-mandated maintenance rather than price, so cheaper maintenance would produce only limited additional work. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI will enhance technicians' productivity without replacing most hands-on duties.

title: Airline and commercial pilots
rationale: AI and advanced automation can improve flight planning, monitoring, communications, and routine aircraft control, potentially reducing some cockpit workload. However, pilots must remain physically present, maintain situational awareness, handle rare emergencies, and bear safety responsibility under stringent certification and crew regulations. Demand is relatively inelastic because pilot labor is only one component of flight costs and air travel is constrained by aircraft, airports, and route demand. Thus, AI will meaningfully assist pilots but is unlikely to reshape or eliminate their core role within the next decade.

title: Animal care and service workers
rationale: Core duties such as feeding, grooming, exercising, restraining, cleaning up after, and training animals require hands-on presence in unpredictable physical settings. AI can improve scheduling, recordkeeping, customer communication, health monitoring, and training recommendations, but robotics is unlikely to replace most direct care economically within the next decade. Lower prices could moderately increase purchases of grooming, sitting, boarding, and training services, although demand remains constrained by pet ownership and the time-intensive nature of care, making the occupation resilient.

title: Announcers and DJs
rationale: AI can already generate scripts, research summaries, playlists, advertisements, voiceovers, and synthetic radio personalities, putting much of broadcast announcing directly in its path. Live party DJs, emcees, interviews, and promotional appearances remain more resistant because they require physical presence, improvisation, and audience rapport, preventing an even higher disruption score. Cheaper production may enable more niche audio programming, but listener attention, advertising revenue, broadcast slots, and the number of live events limit demand expansion. With high disruption and low elasticity, especially in the larger broadcast segment, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount overall.

title: Anthropologists and archeologists
rationale: AI will substantially accelerate literature review, interview transcription and coding, GIS and remote-sensing analysis, artifact classification, data management, and report drafting. However, field observation, excavation, community engagement, contextual interpretation, and compliance judgments still require physical presence and specialized human expertise. Lower costs could enable more cultural and archaeological analysis, but demand remains constrained by research funding, construction activity, preservation regulations, and the finite number of relevant sites and projects. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI reshapes many analytical tasks without replacing its field-based and relational core.

title: Arbitrators, mediators, and conciliators
rationale: The occupation is predominantly language- and analysis-based, allowing AI to review evidence, research relevant rules, summarize testimony, identify settlement options, and draft agreements. However, human neutrality, legitimacy, emotional intelligence, and the ability to manage adversarial discussions remain central, especially in sensitive or binding proceedings. Lower costs could unlock more mediation for disputes that currently go unresolved or proceed to expensive litigation, but the number of disputes and institutional processes limits expansion. High disruption combined with moderate demand elasticity therefore points to restructuring rather than broad replacement.

title: Architects
rationale: Most architectural production—including concept generation, visualization, drafting, code checks, specifications, cost analysis, and BIM documentation—is digital and increasingly automatable with generative design and AI-assisted modeling. Client interpretation, professional liability, multidisciplinary coordination, and construction-site oversight remain human-intensive, preventing full automation. Lower design costs should unlock more iterations and make professional architectural services viable for some smaller projects, but construction demand is constrained by land, financing, permitting, and building costs. The occupation therefore restructures around client advising, design judgment, validation, and project leadership, with fewer hours devoted to routine documentation.

title: Architectural and engineering managers
rationale: AI will materially improve planning, budgeting, scheduling, technical review, risk identification, and progress reporting. However, leadership, personnel decisions, cross-functional negotiation, accountability, and oversight of complex physical projects remain dependent on experienced humans. Lower management costs may enable more engineering and infrastructure projects, but demand is constrained by capital budgets, permitting, and the number of technical teams requiring supervision. Because AI substantially assists rather than overtakes the occupation’s core leadership role, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Archivists, curators, and museum workers
rationale: AI can materially accelerate cataloging, metadata generation, record classification, research, transcription, exhibit writing, and public-reference services, especially for digital archives. However, authentication, acquisition decisions, institutional leadership, public engagement, artifact handling, exhibit installation, and conservation treatments require expert judgment or physical presence. Lower costs could unlock processing of archival backlogs and broader digitization and interpretation, but demand is constrained by museum budgets, collection sizes, and public funding. The occupation is therefore resilient overall, although archivists and desk-based curators will experience substantially more task change than conservators and museum technicians.

title: Art directors
rationale: Art direction is predominantly digital and cognitive, and generative AI already accelerates concept development, image creation, layout exploration, asset variation, and design review. Human judgment remains important for interpreting client goals, maintaining brand coherence, directing teams, negotiating approvals, and coordinating physical productions. Cheaper visual production will enable more campaigns, content variants, and smaller clients to purchase creative services, but the number of senior directors needed will not rise proportionally because each can oversee more output with leaner teams. The occupation therefore will persist, but its tools, workflows, staffing model, and emphasis on strategic creative leadership will change substantially.

title: Assemblers and fabricators
rationale: Most core tasks require physical presence, dexterity, tool use, material handling, and adaptation to real-world variation, limiting direct exposure to purely digital AI. However, AI-enabled vision systems, robotics, quality control, and collaborative robots will increasingly automate repetitive assembly and shift workers toward setup, monitoring, troubleshooting, and complex or low-volume production. Cheaper assembly may support some reshoring and increased manufacturing output, but demand for most finished goods is not elastic enough to rise in proportion to a tenfold productivity gain. Because disruption is meaningful but remains moderate across this broad occupation, the occupation is resilient overall, although routine subfields may experience substantial displacement.

title: Athletes and sports competitors
rationale: Athletes’ core work consists of physical training and authentic human competition in unpredictable real-world settings, which AI cannot substitute for. AI will improve video analysis, opponent scouting, training plans, injury prevention, and tactical decision support, but these tools remain peripheral to performing in events. Demand is constrained by league structures, roster sizes, audience attention, and the rarity of expansion, so productivity improvements would unlock only limited additional employment. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI may enhance performance without substantially reshaping or replacing its core tasks.

title: Athletic trainers
rationale: AI can assist with injury assessment, rehabilitation planning, wearable-data analysis, compliance, and clinical documentation, but most core duties require hands-on treatment, real-time observation, emergency response, and interpersonal judgment. Lower costs could expand access in schools, recreational sports, military settings, and care for active older adults, although licensing rules, institutional budgets, and the need for on-site coverage limit demand growth. Because AI will improve important knowledge-work components without replacing the occupation's physical and relational core, athletic trainers are likely to remain resilient.

title: Atmospheric scientists, including meteorologists
rationale: Most core tasks—analyzing model outputs, coding, preparing forecasts, generating graphics, and communicating findings—are digital and increasingly amenable to AI-assisted automation. Human expertise remains important for severe-weather warnings, novel research, local interpretation, client advice, and accountable public communication. Cheaper, more tailored forecasting could expand demand in logistics, agriculture, energy, insurance, and climate-risk management, but government funding and the limited need for additional general-purpose forecasts constrain that expansion. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity therefore points to restructuring, with fewer routine forecasting tasks and greater emphasis on model supervision, specialized analysis, and decision support.

title: Audiologists
rationale: AI can automate interpretation of hearing tests, documentation, treatment recommendations, and some hearing-aid programming, materially changing the analytical portions of the job. However, physical examination, device fitting, balance assessment, counseling, and work with children or complex patients still require licensed clinicians and direct patient interaction. Demand is relatively elastic because many people with hearing loss remain untreated due to cost and access barriers, while population aging will further expand the potential patient base. With disruption remaining moderate, AI is more likely to improve audiologists’ productivity and reach than to reshape or replace the occupation’s core clinical role.

title: Automotive body and glass repairers
rationale: Core tasks involve hands-on inspection, disassembly, welding, frame alignment, refinishing, and glass installation on uniquely damaged vehicles, making them difficult to automate with AI alone. AI will improve damage assessment, cost estimation, repair planning, parts identification, sensor calibration guidance, and administrative work, but these are supporting rather than dominant tasks. Demand is tied mainly to the number of collisions and damaged vehicles, so cheaper repairs may prevent some vehicles from being totaled and encourage cosmetic work, but will not create a large increase in repair volume. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI will enhance workflows without substantially replacing the physical core of the job.

title: Automotive service technicians and mechanics
rationale: AI can improve fault diagnosis, interpret sensor data, retrieve repair procedures, document work, and communicate estimates, but most core tasks still require physical inspection, dexterity, tools, and hands-on work in varied real-world conditions. Demand is relatively inelastic because vehicle owners will not purchase dramatically more maintenance or repairs merely because technician productivity rises, although lower prices could encourage some preventive work. AI will alter diagnostic workflows and reduce administrative time, but limited near-term robotics capability means it will not substantially automate the occupation's physical core, making the occupation resilient.

title: Bakers
rationale: Baking is predominantly hands-on work involving ingredient handling, dough shaping, oven operation, cleaning, and real-time quality inspection in a physical environment. AI may improve recipe planning, production forecasting, equipment monitoring, and administrative tasks, while advanced automation will have more impact in large commercial facilities than in retail or specialty bakeries. Demand is relatively inelastic because consumers are unlikely to eat dramatically more baked goods even if production becomes much cheaper, although lower costs could support greater variety and customization. Because AI does not substantially reshape the occupation's physical core, bakers remain resilient despite some automation-related pressure.

title: Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists
rationale: Core services require close physical presence, fine motor control, visual judgment, and safe manipulation of highly variable hair, skin, chemicals, and tools. AI can improve appointment scheduling, marketing, recordkeeping, style visualization, and client recommendations, but practical robotic substitution is unlikely to become broadly economical within 10 years. Cheaper and faster services could encourage somewhat more frequent visits and advanced treatments, although hair growth, client time, and customary grooming schedules limit demand expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI primarily improves peripheral business and consultation tasks rather than replacing hands-on service delivery.

title: Bartenders
rationale: Bartending is predominantly physical, customer-facing work requiring real-time drink preparation, cleaning, stocking, social interaction, and judgment about age and intoxication. AI can improve ordering, payments, inventory management, scheduling, and recipe guidance, while automated dispensers may handle standardized drinks, but these tools affect only part of the role. Cheaper and faster service could modestly increase consumption or venue capacity, but demand is constrained by alcohol preferences, regulation, and the number of hospitality occasions, so low disruption makes the occupation resilient.

title: Bill and account collectors
rationale: The occupation is dominated by digital and language-based tasks—locating debtors, making calls, explaining obligations, negotiating standardized payment plans, and documenting interactions—that AI voice agents and automated collection systems can increasingly perform. Humans will remain valuable for complex disputes, emotionally sensitive negotiations, compliance oversight, and escalated cases, but these represent a shrinking share of accounts. Cheaper collection may make pursuing some low-balance debts economical, yet total demand is constrained by the number of delinquent accounts, consumer-protection rules, and creditor policies. Very high disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to replacement and substantial headcount contraction.

title: Biochemists and biophysicists
rationale: AI is increasingly central to literature synthesis, molecular modeling, protein and drug design, data analysis, experimental planning, and scientific writing, substantially changing the occupation’s cognitive tasks. However, laboratory execution, validation, safety oversight, interdisciplinary judgment, and research leadership still require skilled scientists and real-world experimentation. Cheaper and faster discovery should unlock substantial additional research in medicine, agriculture, energy, and environmental protection, although laboratory capacity, funding, regulation, and clinical trials limit expansion. High disruption combined with high latent demand therefore makes augmentation more likely than broad replacement.

title: Bioengineers and biomedical engineers
rationale: AI will substantially accelerate modeling, simulation, literature review, software development, statistical analysis, design optimization, and technical documentation. However, physical prototyping, laboratory experiments, clinical validation, regulatory compliance, equipment support, and collaboration with clinicians and manufacturers remain human-intensive. Lower development costs should enable more biomedical research and product exploration, but regulation, trials, manufacturing, and healthcare budgets limit how fully productivity gains translate into additional demand. The occupation will therefore persist with substantially changed workflows and greater emphasis on experimental judgment, systems integration, validation, and AI-enabled design.

title: Biological technicians
rationale: AI will substantially assist experimental design, data analysis, anomaly detection, documentation, and report writing, while laboratory automation will increasingly handle standardized assays and sample processing. However, technicians still must prepare biological materials, operate and troubleshoot specialized equipment, monitor experiments, maintain contamination controls, and sometimes collect field samples, limiting end-to-end automation. Demand is relatively elastic because cheaper, faster experimentation should enable more biotechnology, pharmaceutical, synthetic-biology, and environmental research, although funding and regulatory constraints prevent unlimited expansion. With disruption remaining moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient, but its work will shift toward instrument oversight, quality control, and handling nonstandard experiments.

title: Boilermakers
rationale: Boilermaking is dominated by physical, site-specific work in hazardous and confined environments, including fitting, welding, cleaning, inspection, and repair. AI can assist with blueprint interpretation, predictive maintenance, defect detection, safety monitoring, and robotic welding, but unstructured worksites and large custom equipment limit substitution for skilled workers. Demand is tied primarily to a relatively fixed stock of boilers, pressure vessels, and industrial facilities, so lower labor costs would generate only modest additional installation or maintenance. The occupation is therefore resilient to AI, although non-AI factors such as declining coal generation may reduce employment.

title: Bookkeeping, accounting, and auditing clerks
rationale: Most core tasks—transaction entry, account classification, reconciliation, report generation, and error checking—are structured digital processes already being automated by accounting platforms and AI. Lower costs may bring better bookkeeping to some small businesses, but demand is largely tied to the number of organizations, transactions, and reporting obligations rather than price, limiting expansion. Because disruption is very high while demand elasticity is low, productivity gains will primarily reduce clerical headcount, with remaining workers shifting toward exception handling, analysis, controls, and client communication.

title: Broadcast, sound, and video technicians
rationale: AI can automate editing, mixing, synchronization, quality monitoring, lighting control, and portions of broadcast operations, materially reducing labor for routine production workflows. However, equipment installation, cabling, rigging, maintenance, troubleshooting, and real-time operation at unpredictable live events still require substantial physical presence and situational judgment. Lower production costs should generate more video, audio, streaming, and event output, but demand is constrained by venue activity, infrastructure budgets, and the number of live productions. The occupation is therefore resilient overall, although digital broadcast and post-production roles will face more restructuring than hands-on audiovisual installation roles.

title: Budget analysts
rationale: Budget analysis is predominantly digital and structured, making consolidation, compliance checks, forecasting, variance analysis, scenario modeling, and report drafting highly amenable to AI. Human judgment will remain important for interpreting policy, negotiating with managers, defending recommendations, and ensuring accountability, but analysts will be able to oversee much larger workloads. Demand is relatively inelastic because organizations prepare a limited number of budgets and government hiring is constrained by appropriations and institutional processes. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount pressure and a replace effect.

title: Bus drivers
rationale: AI will increasingly assist with routing, scheduling, hazard detection, monitoring, and basic passenger information, while autonomous-driving systems may handle portions of predictable routes. However, dense traffic, severe weather, regulatory requirements, passenger emergencies, disability assistance, and supervision of schoolchildren make fully driverless deployment difficult over the next decade. Lower operating costs could support more frequent or expanded transit service, but ridership needs, public budgets, school enrollment, and fixed travel times limit demand expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient overall, although some highly structured routes may be automated or redesigned.

title: Butchers
rationale: Core tasks involve physically handling irregular meat products, making precise cuts, cleaning equipment, lifting stock, and serving customers in person, all of which remain difficult for AI without costly specialized robotics. AI can improve peripheral tasks such as inventory forecasting, ordering, recordkeeping, and food-safety monitoring, while industrial automation may handle standardized processing. Demand is highly inelastic because lower preparation costs would not cause consumers to purchase dramatically more meat, although cheaper custom cuts could generate limited additional demand. Because disruption to the occupation's hands-on core is low, the occupation is resilient despite weak demand elasticity.

title: Calibration technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can automate documentation, scheduling, fault diagnosis, test-plan generation, and analysis of calibration data, while smarter instruments may increasingly support self-calibration. However, much of the core work still requires on-site inspection, physical adjustment, maintenance, dexterity, and responsibility for traceable measurements in varied environments. Demand is anchored to the installed base of equipment, regulatory requirements, and prescribed service intervals, so lower costs may encourage some additional testing but not proportionate expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI will improve productivity and workflows without broadly replacing its hands-on core.

title: Cardiovascular technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can increasingly identify abnormalities in EKG and physiologic data, automate quality checks, draft findings, and streamline patient records. However, much of the occupation requires in-person patient preparation, equipment placement, real-time monitoring, and hands-on assistance during invasive procedures. Lower testing costs may generate some additional use, especially as cardiovascular disease rises, but demand remains constrained by clinical need, physician orders, facilities, and reimbursement. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI will improve analytical and administrative tasks without replacing its core bedside and procedural functions.

title: Career and technical education teachers
rationale: AI can materially assist with lesson planning, personalized instructional materials, grading, progress tracking, and technical simulations. However, the occupation's core also involves demonstrating physical techniques, supervising tools and equipment, enforcing safety procedures, and coaching students in workshops, which require substantial human presence. Cheaper instruction could expand vocational training and adult reskilling, but demand remains constrained by school funding, enrollment, facilities, equipment, and required instructor-to-student ratios. Thus, AI will improve and modify many supporting tasks without reshaping enough of the hands-on core to move the occupation beyond moderate disruption.

title: Carpenters
rationale: Carpentry is dominated by dexterous physical work in varied, often unpredictable jobsites, leaving AI mainly to assist with estimating, blueprint interpretation, measurements, scheduling, and administration. Cheaper and faster carpentry would stimulate additional construction, renovation, customization, and deferred repairs, although land, materials, permits, and overall project budgets limit demand expansion. Because AI is unlikely to reshape the occupation’s hands-on core within the next decade, carpenters remain resilient despite moderate potential for productivity-driven demand growth.

title: Cartographers and photogrammetrists
rationale: Most mapping, image interpretation, feature extraction, data integration, and visualization tasks are digital and increasingly automatable with geospatial AI, although field verification, quality control, and context-specific judgment remain human-intensive. Cheaper production will expand demand for frequently updated, customized, and interactive maps, especially for infrastructure, disaster response, environmental monitoring, and commercial applications. However, government budgets, data-collection costs, licensing requirements, and the finite number of planning projects limit how fully productivity gains translate into additional demand. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-assisted workflows, validation, and higher-level geospatial analysis rather than disappear or expand enough to qualify as augmentation.

title: Cashiers
rationale: Checkout is highly routine and already being automated through self-checkout, computer vision, mobile payment, and cashierless-store systems. Some physical and interpersonal duties remain, including handling unusual items, verifying age, resolving errors, and assisting customers, so disruption is not maximum. Demand for checkout transactions is tied closely to retail sales and will not increase substantially merely because processing becomes cheaper. High disruption combined with highly inelastic demand therefore points to significant headcount contraction.

title: Chefs and head cooks
rationale: AI can assist with menu design, recipe development, purchasing, inventory, scheduling, pricing, and marketing, but the occupation’s core still requires hands-on food evaluation, sensory judgment, and real-time leadership in a physical kitchen. Robotics may automate some standardized preparation, yet varied ingredients, crowded workspaces, and unpredictable service conditions limit near-term substitution. Cheaper chef-level planning could help more establishments offer sophisticated menus, but demand remains constrained by consumer dining frequency, restaurant capacity, and the physical costs of food and service. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient even as administrative and planning tasks become more AI-enabled.

title: Chemical engineers
rationale: AI will substantially assist process simulation, equipment design, optimization, research synthesis, cost estimation, compliance documentation, and fault diagnosis. However, laboratory validation, plant-specific troubleshooting, safety judgment, regulatory accountability, and collaboration with operators require physical-world expertise and human oversight. Cheaper engineering could support more process improvements and materials research, but demand remains constrained by manufacturing investment, regulation, and demand for the underlying products. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI reshapes many analytical tasks without fully transforming its hands-on, safety-critical core.

title: Chemical technicians
rationale: AI can substantially assist with experimental design, instrument-data interpretation, anomaly detection, documentation, and report generation. However, core duties still involve hands-on sample preparation, equipment operation and maintenance, chemical handling, and troubleshooting in laboratories or manufacturing facilities. Cheaper and faster testing could expand materials research, product development, environmental monitoring, and quality assurance, although demand remains partly tied to manufacturing volumes and regulatory requirements. Because AI reshapes the analytical portions without eliminating the occupation’s physical laboratory core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Chemists and materials scientists
rationale: AI will substantially reshape literature review, molecular and materials design, simulation, experimental planning, instrument-data analysis, and technical reporting. However, physical sample preparation, laboratory execution, safety oversight, troubleshooting, and real-world validation will continue to require scientists and technicians, limiting full automation. Demand is relatively elastic because cheaper and faster discovery would enable more candidate drugs, materials, formulations, and testing projects, although laboratory capacity, regulation, and commercialization costs constrain expansion. High disruption combined with high elasticity therefore points to augmentation, with scientists overseeing larger AI-assisted experimental portfolios and producing more discoveries per worker.

title: Childcare workers
rationale: Core duties such as hands-on supervision, feeding, hygiene, emotional support, and emergency response require trusted human presence and cannot be delegated readily to AI. AI can assist with lesson planning, parent communication, scheduling, documentation, and developmental screening, but staffing-ratio rules further limit labor substitution. Demand has moderate elasticity because lower prices could move care from unpaid or informal arrangements into paid settings and increase hours consumed, although birth rates and the finite number of children constrain expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI improving peripheral administrative and educational tasks rather than reshaping the core job.

title: Chiropractors
rationale: Core chiropractic work requires in-person physical examination, manual dexterity, patient positioning, and hands-on spinal or joint manipulation, all of which remain difficult for AI to perform. AI can assist with imaging interpretation, documentation, treatment planning, patient education, scheduling, and practice marketing, but these are secondary to physical care. Lower prices and greater efficiency could unlock moderate additional demand given widespread musculoskeletal pain and interest in non-drug treatment, although demand remains limited by patient preferences, clinical need, and reimbursement. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI will improve peripheral cognitive and administrative tasks without substantially replacing its hands-on core.

title: Civil engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: AI-enabled CAD, automated quantity and cost estimation, plan review, data analysis, and report generation will materially accelerate the occupation's office-based tasks. However, field surveys, materials testing, site inspections, instrument setup, and coordination with engineers and construction crews still require real-world presence and contextual judgment. Cheaper technical support could enable more infrastructure design and maintenance, but public budgets, permitting, construction capacity, and project timelines limit demand expansion. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient, although its task mix will shift toward field verification, quality control, and oversight of automated outputs.

title: Civil engineers
rationale: AI-enabled CAD, generative design, simulation, cost estimation, code review, permitting documentation, and project monitoring will materially reshape a large share of civil engineers’ analytical and administrative work. Disruption is limited by site-specific judgment, stakeholder coordination, field oversight, safety liability, and licensed engineers’ responsibility for approving designs. Cheaper engineering may enable more design alternatives and make some infrastructure projects feasible, but demand remains constrained by public funding, permitting, land, and construction capacity. The occupation therefore fits restructure: engineers will remain essential, but their work will shift toward validation, systems judgment, risk ownership, and oversight of AI-generated designs.

title: Claims adjusters, appraisers, examiners, and investigators
rationale: Much of claims handling consists of digital document review, policy interpretation, image-based damage estimation, fraud screening, report generation, and payment recommendations, all of which are increasingly automatable with AI. Human involvement will remain important for physical inspections, interviews, negotiation, surveillance, and complex or disputed claims, but fewer workers will be able to process a given caseload. Demand is largely determined by the volume of insured losses rather than the cost of claims administration, so cheaper processing will not generate many additional claims, making significant headcount contraction likely.

title: Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians
rationale: AI will increasingly automate result interpretation, anomaly detection, documentation, quality monitoring, and portions of complex image- and sequence-based analysis. However, specimen preparation, equipment calibration and troubleshooting, contamination control, and hands-on work with biohazardous materials still require substantial laboratory presence and dexterity. Cheaper testing could expand screening, genetic analysis, and disease monitoring, but demand remains constrained by clinical utility, physician ordering, reimbursement, and specimen-collection requirements. The occupation is therefore resilient under the rubric, although routine technician roles will face more workflow redesign than specialized technologist roles.

title: Coaches and scouts
rationale: AI will materially improve video analysis, performance tracking, opponent research, training-plan design, and the initial screening of scouting prospects. However, conducting practices, correcting physical technique, motivating athletes, building trust, recruiting, and making context-sensitive decisions during competitions still require substantial human presence and interpersonal skill. Cheaper analytics and personalized training could expand recreational instruction and allow more teams to access sophisticated coaching, although the number of roster, school, and professional-team positions remains structurally limited. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI reshapes important analytical tasks but does not displace the human-centered core of coaching.

title: Community health workers
rationale: AI can materially streamline documentation, case tracking, translation, resource matching, health education materials, and routine client follow-up. However, outreach, home visits, basic screenings, advocacy, culturally grounded trust, and empathetic support require human presence and community relationships. Demand is highly latent because many underserved populations lack navigation and preventive support, although public funding and program capacity will limit expansion. Because AI changes supporting workflows more than the occupation’s relationship-centered core, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Compensation and benefits managers
rationale: The occupation is predominantly cognitive and digital: AI can automate compensation benchmarking, benefits-cost analysis, regulatory monitoring, plan modeling, employee communications, and presentation preparation. Human judgment, executive consultation, vendor negotiation, leadership, and accountability will remain important, but AI-enabled analytics platforms and outside providers can let fewer managers oversee larger programs. Demand is relatively inelastic because each organization needs only a limited number of compensation and benefits programs, and cheaper analysis will not create proportionally more need for managerial oversight. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to headcount contraction and a replace effect.

title: Compensation, benefits, and job analysis specialists
rationale: Most core tasks are digital and cognitive, including benchmarking pay, analyzing costs, monitoring regulations, classifying jobs, and drafting reports and position descriptions, all of which AI can substantially automate. Human judgment will remain important for sensitive policy decisions, stakeholder negotiations, legal accountability, and organization-specific context. Demand may expand somewhat through more frequent and granular analysis, but each organization needs only a limited number of compensation and benefits programs, so productivity gains are likely to reduce specialist headcount.

title: Compliance officers
rationale: Most compliance work involves analyzing regulations, reviewing documents, monitoring controls, assessing risks, and producing policies, reports, and training materials—all tasks directly affected by current AI systems. Human judgment, legal accountability, investigations, stakeholder communication, and occasional onsite inspections will remain important, but fewer officers may be able to oversee much larger compliance workloads. Cheaper compliance could enable more continuous monitoring and improve access for smaller organizations, yet demand is largely determined by the number of regulated entities and mandatory requirements rather than price. Thus, high disruption combined with relatively low demand elasticity points to headcount contraction and a replace outcome.

title: Computer and information research scientists
rationale: Nearly all core tasks are digital and cognitive, including coding, modeling, literature review, experimental design, data analysis, and technical writing, making them highly exposed to increasingly capable AI research tools. Human researchers will remain important for selecting consequential problems, judging novel results, coordinating multidisciplinary work, and validating systems, but their workflows and required skills will change substantially. Demand is highly elastic because cheaper computing research enables more software, AI, cybersecurity, robotics, and scientific applications, while rapid technological competition encourages greater R&D investment. High disruption combined with strong expansion in valuable research output supports an augment classification.

title: Computer and information systems managers
rationale: AI will materially automate project analysis, budgeting, documentation, system monitoring, vendor evaluation, and technical decision support. However, organizational accountability, cross-functional negotiation, personnel leadership, cybersecurity governance, and context-specific prioritization will remain substantially human-led. Lower management costs and rapid growth in AI, cloud, cybersecurity, and digital infrastructure will create additional projects, but managerial demand is constrained by organizational scale and wider AI-enabled spans of control. The occupation therefore will persist and likely grow in important segments, while shifting toward AI governance, strategic judgment, and leadership of more productive technical teams.

title: Computer hardware engineers
rationale: Most design, simulation, verification, test analysis, and documentation tasks are digital and increasingly improved by AI-enabled electronic design automation, although laboratory validation and manufacturing oversight still require physical-world expertise. Faster and cheaper engineering should unlock substantial demand for custom chips, AI accelerators, connected devices, automotive systems, and specialized embedded hardware. Fabrication costs, long production cycles, and reliability requirements limit elasticity somewhat, but expanding hardware applications should absorb much of the productivity gain. The occupation is therefore likely to be augmented, with engineers producing more designs while shifting toward system architecture, validation, and AI-tool supervision.

title: Computer network architects
rationale: Network architecture is predominantly digital knowledge work, and AI can increasingly generate configurations, analyze traffic, document systems, simulate designs, and diagnose faults. Human architects will remain important for security tradeoffs, organization-specific requirements, deployment oversight, vendor coordination, and accountability in complex failures. Cheaper architecture will support more cloud, edge, cybersecurity, and AI infrastructure, but demand is constrained by the finite number of organizations and networks, so output is unlikely to rise in proportion to productivity. The occupation therefore is likely to persist and grow in advanced segments while shifting toward higher-level design, validation, governance, and integration.

title: Computer programmers
rationale: Programming is almost entirely digital, and AI coding tools already generate, translate, test, debug, and document code, directly affecting nearly every core task. Cheaper code will stimulate more software creation and modernization, but demand for narrowly defined programmers is constrained as routine implementation is automated and higher-level work shifts to software developers and engineers. The occupation therefore faces substantial skill and role changes, with remaining programmers moving toward architecture, requirements interpretation, system integration, validation, and oversight of AI-generated code.

title: Computer support specialists
rationale: Most user-support work consists of digital diagnosis, documentation, and step-by-step guidance that AI agents can already automate, although onsite hardware work and complex network troubleshooting remain less exposed. Cheaper support may encourage organizations to offer broader or faster assistance, but demand is primarily constrained by the number of users, devices, and technical incidents rather than service cost. Because disruption is high while demand expansion is limited, AI is likely to reduce overall headcount and concentrate remaining workers in complex, security-sensitive, and hands-on cases.

title: Computer systems analysts
rationale: Most systems-analysis tasks are digital and cognitive, including requirements analysis, technology research, system design, documentation, testing, and some programming, making them highly amenable to AI assistance. Human judgment remains important for eliciting ambiguous business needs, navigating organizational constraints, coordinating stakeholders, and overseeing implementation. Cheaper and faster analysis should unlock substantial demand from modernization backlogs, system integration, cybersecurity needs, and adoption of AI itself, although organizational capacity will constrain expansion. High disruption combined with high demand elasticity therefore points to augmentation, with analysts producing more and shifting toward architecture, governance, and stakeholder management.

title: Concierges
rationale: AI assistants and apps can automate many information-heavy duties, including recommendations, reservations, travel planning, messaging, and routing service requests. However, greeting people, handling packages and errands, resolving unexpected on-site problems, and providing trusted interpersonal service still require a physical presence. Demand is constrained by the number of hotels, residences, and offices rather than by the cost of producing concierge advice, so cheaper service is unlikely to generate proportionally more jobs. Because AI will substantially alter but not fully overtake the occupation's on-site core, the occupation is resilient at the upper boundary of moderate disruption.

title: Conservation scientists and foresters
rationale: AI will materially improve satellite and drone-image analysis, GIS mapping, wildfire modeling, inventory estimation, regulatory documentation, and management-plan development. However, field inspection, work in remote and hazardous terrain, fire response, stakeholder negotiation, and supervision of land-management activities still require substantial human presence and judgment. Lower costs could enable more frequent monitoring and management of currently underserved forests and rangelands, although government budgets, regulation, and the finite land base limit demand expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI enhances a sizable knowledge-work component without replacing its field-based core.

title: Construction and building inspectors
rationale: AI can automate plan review, code lookup, report drafting, image analysis, scheduling, and parts of remote inspection, materially changing the office-based portion of the job. However, core duties still require accountable onsite observation, testing equipment, access to difficult spaces, and judgment about varied real-world conditions. Demand is tied mainly to construction activity and legally required inspection cycles, so cheaper inspections would generate only limited additional volume. With moderate disruption rather than wholesale automation, the occupation is resilient, although inspectors will increasingly use AI, drones, and remote-inspection tools.

title: Construction equipment operators
rationale: AI-enabled machine guidance, autonomous grading and excavation, collision avoidance, and predictive maintenance will materially change equipment operation, especially on repetitive, well-mapped sites. However, variable terrain, safety risks, coordination with crews, equipment servicing, and work in changing environments will continue to require substantial human presence and judgment. Cheaper operation may enable somewhat more infrastructure and construction, but demand is constrained by project budgets, permitting, land, materials, and broader construction activity, so it will not expand proportionally. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient, although operators will increasingly supervise automated equipment and use digital control systems.

title: Construction laborers and helpers
rationale: Core duties involve strenuous physical work, tool use, material handling, and adaptation to varied, hazardous jobsites, all of which remain difficult for AI and robotics to automate. AI may improve scheduling, safety monitoring, measurements, training, and equipment operation, while prefabrication may reduce selected helper tasks. Cheaper construction labor could unlock meaningful additional building, renovation, and infrastructure activity, although land, permitting, financing, and material constraints limit demand expansion. Because disruption to the occupation's hands-on core is low, the occupation is resilient.

title: Construction managers
rationale: AI will materially improve estimating, scheduling, contract review, progress reporting, risk detection, and coordination across project data. However, core responsibilities still require onsite observation, accountability, negotiations, leadership, and rapid judgment amid unpredictable physical conditions. More efficient management may enable firms to oversee additional projects, but construction demand remains constrained by financing, land, permits, materials, and skilled labor. Because AI substantially assists the digital portions without replacing the field-based managerial core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Cooks
rationale: Core cooking tasks require physical dexterity, sensory judgment, sanitation, and real-time coordination in crowded kitchens, placing most of the work outside the direct reach of current AI. AI can assist with recipes, inventory, scheduling, order sequencing, and quality monitoring, while specialized kitchen robotics may reduce staffing in standardized fast-food and short-order settings. Demand could expand somewhat if preparation became cheaper, but food consumption is bounded and labor is only one component of meal prices, limiting the headcount benefit. Because disruption remains low for the occupation overall, cooks are resilient despite greater automation risk in highly standardized segments.

title: Correctional officers and bailiffs
rationale: Core duties require continuous physical presence, situational judgment, interpersonal authority, and the ability to respond to disturbances or restrain and escort people. AI can improve surveillance, threat detection, facility inspections, scheduling, and report writing, but legal accountability and unpredictable confrontations limit substitution over the next decade. Demand is tied primarily to incarcerated populations, courtroom activity, security requirements, and government budgets, so cheaper monitoring would not generate substantially more correctional or bailiff services. The occupation is therefore resilient to AI-driven task replacement, although technology may reduce staffing needs at the margin and alter monitoring and administrative work.

title: Cost estimators
rationale: Most estimating tasks—reading digital plans, extracting quantities, comparing cost databases, modeling scenarios, and drafting bids—are directly amenable to AI integrated with BIM and CAD software. Human judgment, site visits, stakeholder coordination, and responsibility for unusual project risks remain important, preventing full automation. Demand is linked primarily to the number of construction and manufacturing projects, so cheaper estimates may generate more bid scenarios but will not produce a proportional increase in projects. High disruption combined with limited demand expansion points to fewer estimators handling more work, making replace the best fit.

title: Court reporters and simultaneous captioners
rationale: Speech recognition, speaker diarization, punctuation, and transcript editing are almost entirely digital tasks already handled increasingly well by AI, placing the occupation directly in its path. Human expertise will remain important for certifying legal records, resolving inaudible or ambiguous speech, identifying speakers, and documenting gestures and exhibits, but these functions can shift toward supervising automated transcription. Demand for legal records is tied largely to the number of proceedings, while cheaper captioning may unlock some additional accessibility use but probably not enough to offset large productivity gains. Consequently, fewer professionals are likely to oversee more proceedings and captioning sessions, making replacement the most likely net effect.

title: Craft and fine artists
rationale: AI can substantially accelerate ideation, sketching, digital illustration, portfolio creation, marketing, and grant writing, placing commercial illustrators and digital artists under particular pressure. However, much of the occupation involves physically manipulating materials, operating specialized equipment, and producing handmade objects whose provenance and human authorship are part of their value. Lower production costs could expand demand for customized imagery and art products, but discretionary spending, limited buyer attention, and the scarcity value of original work constrain that expansion. Because disruption is significant but does not broadly replace the occupation's hands-on core, the aggregate occupation is resilient, with substantial restructuring in its digital specialties.

title: Credit counselors
rationale: Most core tasks—collecting financial data, assessing budgets and debts, generating repayment plans, explaining options, and drafting communications—are digital and increasingly automatable with AI. Human counselors remain important for trust, empathy, complex negotiations, regulatory accountability, and clients in financial distress. Lower costs could extend counseling to many underserved borrowers, but demand is constrained by clients’ ability to pay, institutional budgets, and the finite number of debt problems requiring intervention. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around oversight, relationship management, and difficult cases rather than disappear.

title: Customer service representatives
rationale: Most customer-service tasks are language-based, digitally mediated, and structured around retrieving information, updating accounts, processing transactions, and documenting interactions—all capabilities increasingly handled by conversational AI and automated workflows. Humans will remain important for complex, regulated, emotionally charged, or face-to-face cases, but these represent a shrinking share of contacts as AI improves. Demand has low elasticity because service volume is largely tied to the number of customers and transactions, and cheaper support is unlikely to generate enough additional contacts to offset large productivity gains. The combination of very high disruption and limited demand expansion makes replace the appropriate category.

title: Dancers and choreographers
rationale: Dancing is fundamentally embodied, physical, and dependent on athletic skill, rehearsal, teamwork, and live or on-set presence, while choreography also requires hands-on demonstration and direction. AI can assist choreographers with music selection, routine ideation, motion visualization, marketing, and administration, and synthetic performers may substitute for some dancers in digital media, but these tools do not replace most core work. Cheaper production and choreography could expand online dance content, instruction, and performances, although audience attention, arts funding, and demand for live events limit the headcount response. Because disruption remains low despite moderate demand elasticity, the occupation is resilient.

title: Data scientists
rationale: Data science is almost entirely digital and cognitive, and AI already accelerates coding, data cleaning, exploratory analysis, model development, visualization, and report writing. Human judgment remains important for defining questions, evaluating data quality and causality, validating models, applying domain knowledge, and advising stakeholders. Demand is relatively elastic because cheaper analysis enables more organizations and teams to exploit growing datasets, develop AI products, and analyze decisions that previously did not justify dedicated resources. With very high disruption but strong expansion in analytical use cases, the occupation is likely to be augmented while its tools and required skills change substantially.

title: Database administrators and architects
rationale: The work is almost entirely digital, and AI can already generate SQL, propose schemas, diagnose performance issues, automate monitoring, and assist with migrations, backups, and permissions. Demand will expand as AI adoption creates more data-intensive systems requiring reliable architecture, governance, security, and integration, but cloud platforms and managed database services allow fewer administrators to support more infrastructure. This moderate elasticity is unlikely to preserve routine DBA work fully, while higher-level architecture and data-platform responsibilities should grow. The occupation therefore restructures toward design, governance, security, and oversight as routine administration becomes increasingly automated.

title: Delivery truck drivers and driver/sales workers
rationale: AI already improves routing, dispatch, scheduling, sales support, and delivery documentation, while autonomous-driving systems may increasingly handle portions of routine routes. However, loading, unloading, navigating difficult last-mile environments, handling exceptions, and interacting with customers still require physical presence and adaptable human judgment. Cheaper delivery would stimulate additional e-commerce and on-demand services, but demand remains bounded by purchases of physical goods and congestion, so the occupation is resilient despite meaningful changes to its workflows.

title: Dental and ophthalmic laboratory technicians and medical appliance technicians
rationale: The occupation combines hands-on precision fabrication, finishing, repair, and quality inspection with increasingly digital design, automated machining, computer vision, and 3D printing. AI-enabled design and manufacturing systems will substantially streamline standardized dental and ophthalmic production, but customized fitting, material handling, troubleshooting, and final adjustments remain difficult to automate fully. Demand may increase somewhat as lower costs improve access to dental restorations and medical appliances, but prescriptions, patient need, and replacement cycles limit how much consumption can expand. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high across the combined occupation, the net effect is resilient, although routine production roles are likely to decline and shift toward equipment operation and customization.

title: Dental assistants
rationale: Most core tasks require chairside presence, manual dexterity, infection control, equipment handling, and direct patient interaction, making them difficult to automate with software-based AI. AI can streamline scheduling, billing, records, patient instructions, and x-ray quality checks, but these are only part of the role. Cheaper, more efficient assisting could modestly expand dental capacity and access, although demand remains constrained by dentists’ capacity, insurance coverage, regulation, and the need for in-person treatment. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI primarily improves peripheral administrative and diagnostic-support tasks rather than replacing its hands-on core.

title: Dental hygienists
rationale: Core duties such as scaling and polishing teeth, applying sealants, positioning patients, and performing clinical examinations require licensed, hands-on work, fine motor control, and in-person interaction. AI can improve x-ray interpretation, documentation, scheduling, risk assessment, and patient education, but these are supporting rather than dominant tasks. Cheaper, faster care could unlock meaningful demand among underserved populations, although preventive-care frequency, insurance coverage, regulation, and clinic capacity limit expansion, so low disruption makes the occupation resilient.

title: Dentists
rationale: Dentistry centers on licensed, hands-on procedures requiring fine motor control, patient management, and physical presence, keeping disruption low. AI will increasingly assist with imaging interpretation, treatment planning, documentation, scheduling, and appliance design, but it is unlikely to perform most chairside treatment autonomously within the next decade. Lower costs and faster workflows could unlock meaningful demand for deferred, preventive, restorative, and cosmetic care, although biological need, insurance coverage, and chair capacity limit expansion. Because AI primarily improves supporting cognitive and administrative tasks rather than replacing the procedural core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Desktop publishers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks—page layout, image editing, text formatting, proofreading, and file preparation—are digital and increasingly automated by generative design tools, templates, and publishing software. Cheaper production may lead organizations to create more materials, but demand for formal page-layout work is constrained by declining print publishing and by self-service tools that let writers, editors, and designers perform it themselves. Because disruption is very high while demand elasticity is low, productivity gains are likely to reduce specialized desktop-publisher headcount rather than generate enough additional work to offset automation.

title: Diagnostic medical sonographers
rationale: AI can increasingly automate measurements, flag abnormalities, assess image quality, and guide probe placement, materially changing the analytical and technical portions of sonography. However, obtaining diagnostic images still requires in-person patient positioning, adaptive hand–eye coordination, probe manipulation, and compassionate interaction, especially in difficult clinical cases. Cheaper and faster ultrasound could expand screening, point-of-care imaging, and access in underserved settings, but medical necessity, reimbursement, and clinician capacity limit demand growth. The occupation is therefore resilient: AI will improve workflow and throughput without replacing its hands-on core over the next decade.

title: Diesel service technicians and mechanics
rationale: The occupation is dominated by hands-on inspection, disassembly, repair, replacement, and testing of heavy equipment in varied physical settings. AI will improve fault diagnosis, technical-manual retrieval, work planning, and predictive maintenance, but technicians must still verify problems and execute repairs with tools, dexterity, and physical presence. Demand is relatively inelastic because repair volume is driven mainly by fleet size, vehicle mileage, breakdowns, and maintenance requirements, although lower costs could reduce deferred maintenance. The core physical work therefore remains resilient even as AI substantially improves diagnostic support and shop efficiency.

title: Dietitians and nutritionists
rationale: AI can substantially automate nutritional assessments, meal-plan generation, research synthesis, documentation, educational materials, and routine monitoring, although complex clinical judgment, accountability, and behavior-change counseling still benefit from licensed human professionals. Demand is relatively elastic because personalized nutrition and preventive counseling are currently constrained by cost and access, while obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and population aging create a large pool of unmet need. High disruption combined with high latent demand makes augmentation most likely, with dietitians serving more clients while focusing on complex cases, motivation, and care coordination.

title: Drafters
rationale: Drafting is almost entirely digital, structured work performed in CAD and BIM, placing core tasks such as generating drawings, adding details, checking dimensions, and revising models directly in AI's path. Generative design and automated modeling will sharply increase productivity and allow architects and engineers to perform more drafting themselves, although human review remains important for technical accuracy, codes, manufacturability, and project-specific coordination. Lower design costs should stimulate additional customization and some new construction and manufacturing work, but demand is constrained by physical investment, permitting, and engineering-project volumes. High disruption combined with moderate demand elasticity therefore points to restructuring, with fewer routine CAD operators and greater demand for drafters who provide domain expertise, validation, and multidisciplinary BIM coordination.

title: Drywall installers, ceiling tile installers, and tapers
rationale: Core tasks require physical strength, dexterity, mobility, and adaptation to irregular conditions at changing construction sites, placing them largely beyond near-term AI capabilities. AI may improve estimating, measurements, scheduling, and plan interpretation, while specialized tools or robotics could automate portions of taping and finishing, but these advances affect only a limited share of the work. Cheaper installation would modestly encourage remodeling and construction, although demand remains constrained by the number of buildings and broader construction activity. Because disruption to the hands-on core is low, the occupation is resilient.

title: Economists
rationale: Economists perform predominantly digital and cognitive tasks—including literature review, statistical coding, model development, forecasting, data interpretation, and report writing—that AI can already accelerate substantially. Cheaper analysis should enable organizations to evaluate more policies, markets, and business decisions, but demand is constrained by government budgets, limited decision-making needs, and the importance of expert judgment and credibility. High disruption combined with moderate demand expansion points to restructuring, with economists shifting toward model validation, causal reasoning, problem formulation, and communication while fewer hours are devoted to routine analysis and drafting.

title: Editors
rationale: Editing is almost entirely digital and language-based, and current AI systems can already perform proofreading, rewriting, summarization, style enforcement, headline generation, and preliminary fact-checking. Human judgment remains important for publication strategy, ethics, source reliability, audience fit, and managing writers, but editors will increasingly supervise AI-generated revisions rather than execute every edit themselves. Lower costs will allow more books, websites, marketing materials, and specialized content to receive editorial review, although limited publishing budgets and audience attention constrain demand expansion. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity therefore points to restructuring, with fewer routine copy-editing roles and greater emphasis on judgment, domain expertise, and editorial direction.

title: Electrical and electronic engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can accelerate circuit drafting, test-data analysis, fault diagnosis, documentation, and design-quality review. However, much of the core work involves physically assembling prototypes, operating instruments, calibrating equipment, inspecting production conditions, and repairing hardware in laboratories or factories. Cheaper engineering support may encourage more electronics development and testing, but demand is constrained by physical production cycles, capital costs, and increasing automation of manual tasks. The occupation is therefore moderately disrupted but remains resilient because hands-on work and real-world troubleshooting prevent AI from reshaping the entire role.

title: Electrical and electronics engineers
rationale: AI will materially accelerate circuit and system design, simulation, optimization, documentation, requirements analysis, and troubleshooting, making much of the occupation’s computer-based engineering work substantially more productive. However, physical testing, safety validation, site-specific problem solving, manufacturing oversight, and professional accountability will continue to require engineers. Cheaper engineering should unlock additional demand across electrification, semiconductors, communications, automation, renewable energy, and advanced electronics, allowing expanded output to absorb much of the productivity gain. Therefore, the occupation is likely to be augmented, with engineers producing more and shifting toward validation, integration, and higher-level design decisions.

title: Electrical and electronics installers and repairers
rationale: AI-assisted diagnostics, predictive-maintenance systems, remote monitoring, and automated documentation will materially improve troubleshooting and preparation. However, installation, disassembly, component replacement, testing, and work in awkward or hazardous environments still require skilled physical presence. Demand is tied largely to the installed equipment base and actual maintenance needs, so lower costs may encourage some preventive maintenance and repair instead of replacement but will not generate proportionate growth in service volume; therefore, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Electrical power-line installers and repairers
rationale: Core tasks involve hazardous, physically demanding fieldwork on varied infrastructure and in unpredictable weather, putting them largely beyond AI software and near-term robotics. AI can improve outage diagnosis, remote inspection, maintenance scheduling, crew dispatch, and training, but it cannot readily perform pole climbing, cable installation, or emergency repairs. Cheaper labor could modestly accelerate grid modernization and electrification projects, although capital costs, regulation, and finite infrastructure needs limit demand expansion; therefore, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Electricians
