rationale: Electricians’ core work consists of hands-on installation, inspection, troubleshooting, and repair in varied, hazardous worksites, making it difficult for AI or robotics to automate over the next decade. AI can improve peripheral and cognitive tasks such as blueprint interpretation, code lookup, diagnostics, estimating, scheduling, and documentation, but a licensed worker will generally remain responsible for physical execution and safety. Demand has moderate expansion potential because lower costs could encourage upgrades, electrification, renewable-energy connections, and smart-building installations, although construction cycles, permitting, and the finite stock of buildings impose limits. With disruption below 7, the occupation is resilient even as AI-enabled tools raise individual productivity.

title: Electro-mechanical and mechatronics technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can materially assist with interpreting schematics, analyzing test data, diagnosing faults, generating reports, and planning maintenance. However, core duties still require onsite inspection, precision measurement, calibration, fabrication, soldering, and physical repair of varied equipment. Cheaper and faster technician services could support broader adoption of robotics and predictive maintenance, but demand remains constrained by the installed base of industrial equipment and manufacturing investment. Therefore, AI will improve workflows without eliminating the occupation's hands-on core, making it resilient.

title: Elementary, middle, and high school principals
rationale: AI can substantially streamline scheduling, budgeting, reporting, achievement-data analysis, policy drafting, and routine communications. However, principals' core responsibilities also require in-person leadership, conflict resolution, student discipline, staff evaluation, community trust, and legal accountability in unpredictable school environments. Demand is highly inelastic because schools generally need a fixed number of accountable leaders, typically one principal per school, and cheaper administration would not cause many more schools or principal services to be consumed. The occupation is therefore resilient: workflows will change meaningfully, but AI is unlikely to displace the human leadership role at its core.

title: Elevator and escalator installers and repairers
rationale: Core tasks require licensed workers to travel to equipment, work in hazardous and confined spaces, manipulate heavy components, connect wiring, and perform physical repairs. AI-enabled diagnostics, predictive maintenance, blueprint interpretation, and service-record automation will improve troubleshooting and preparation, but robotics is unlikely to replace the varied onsite work within ten years. Demand is constrained by the installed base, construction activity, inspection requirements, and maintenance schedules, so cheaper service would generate only limited additional work. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI primarily augmenting technicians rather than reshaping or eliminating their core role.

title: Emergency management directors
rationale: AI will materially improve hazard analysis, scenario modeling, plan drafting, resource allocation, public communications, and post-disaster assessments. However, the core role also requires accountable decision-making under uncertainty, interagency trust, leadership, public-facing communication, and real-world command presence during crises. Demand is relatively inelastic because staffing is tied to the number of jurisdictions and institutions, public budgets, and formal authority structures rather than the volume of plans produced. The occupation is therefore resilient: AI will significantly enhance planning and administrative work but is unlikely to replace the human director's leadership and responsibility.

title: EMTs and paramedics
rationale: AI can improve dispatch, clinical decision support, EKG interpretation, documentation, and communication with hospitals. However, the core work requires rapid physical response, hands-on treatment, patient movement, transport, and judgment in unpredictable and hazardous environments. Demand is tied mainly to the incidence and location of emergencies, so lower costs may improve coverage and response times but will not generate proportionally more calls. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI will assist crews without replacing their essential real-world presence.

title: Entertainment and recreation managers
rationale: AI will substantially assist with scheduling, budgeting, program design, marketing, customer-feedback analysis, hiring administration, and routine communications. However, core responsibilities still require on-site oversight, safety judgment, staff leadership, customer interaction, and rapid responses to unpredictable operational problems. Cheaper management could support more activities and improve offerings, but demand remains constrained by physical facilities, participant interest, staffing, and local budgets, so moderate expansion is likely without fundamentally displacing the occupation.

title: Environmental engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can automate sample-data analysis, compliance-document review, reporting, scheduling, and recordkeeping, while smarter sensors and testing systems will reduce some routine monitoring work. However, collecting samples, operating and cleaning equipment, inspecting facilities, handling hazardous materials, and responding to unexpected field conditions require physical presence and practical judgment. Demand is constrained by regulation, public budgets, and the number of environmental remediation and infrastructure projects, so lower costs will generate only limited additional work. Because AI changes the analytical and administrative portions without replacing the field-intensive core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Environmental engineers
rationale: AI will materially accelerate data analysis, modeling, report and permit preparation, compliance review, and preliminary system design. However, field inspections, site-specific troubleshooting, stakeholder coordination, regulatory judgment, and licensed responsibility for safety-critical designs continue to require human engineers. Cheaper engineering could enable more remediation, pollution-control, and water-infrastructure projects, but demand remains constrained by regulation, construction budgets, and public funding. Because disruption stops short of reshaping the occupation’s field-based and accountable core, the occupation is resilient despite meaningful AI augmentation.

title: Environmental science and protection technicians
rationale: AI can automate data review, contaminant pattern detection, compliance checks, report drafting, and interpretation of sensor outputs. However, core duties still involve site inspections, equipment setup, sample collection, chain-of-custody procedures, laboratory handling, and judgment in unpredictable physical environments. Cheaper monitoring and analysis could expand testing coverage and continuous environmental surveillance, although regulation, public budgets, and the cost of fieldwork constrain that expansion. Because AI substantially assists the analytical portions without replacing the occupation's field and laboratory core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Environmental scientists and specialists
rationale: AI will materially accelerate data analysis, pollution modeling, regulatory review, literature synthesis, and technical report preparation. However, site investigations, sampling design, laboratory and field coordination, stakeholder communication, and context-sensitive scientific judgment still require substantial human involvement and real-world presence. Cheaper analysis could expand environmental monitoring and consulting, but demand remains constrained by regulation, government budgets, permitting activity, and the number of physical projects and contaminated sites. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient even as its office-based workflows become substantially more AI-assisted.

title: Epidemiologists
rationale: AI can substantially accelerate literature review, statistical programming, disease surveillance, predictive modeling, report writing, and grant preparation, all of which constitute a large share of epidemiologists’ knowledge work. Human expertise remains essential for study design, causal inference, data-quality assessment, field investigations, community engagement, ethical judgment, and public-health accountability. Lower costs could expand surveillance and research, especially for emerging diseases and underserved populations, but government budgets, access to reliable data, and institutional constraints limit demand growth. The occupation therefore is likely to be restructured around AI-enabled analysis and higher-level scientific judgment rather than broadly eliminated.

title: Exercise physiologists
rationale: AI can substantially assist with medical-history review, physiological data analysis, documentation, risk screening, and personalized exercise-plan generation. However, core duties still involve in-person testing, safe supervision, equipment use, clinical judgment, motivation, and empathetic interaction with patients who may have serious health conditions. Lower costs could expand access to personalized exercise and chronic-disease management, although reimbursement constraints and the need for hands-on care limit demand growth. Because AI primarily augments the cognitive portions without replacing the occupation’s physical and interpersonal core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Farmers, ranchers, and other agricultural managers
rationale: AI will materially improve crop and livestock monitoring, yield forecasting, market analysis, recordkeeping, and precision-agriculture decisions. However, equipment maintenance, animal care, worker supervision, and responses to unpredictable field conditions still require substantial physical presence and practical judgment. Demand for agricultural output is relatively inelastic, so productivity gains are more likely to reinforce farm consolidation than generate proportionally more managerial jobs, but the occupation remains resilient because AI does not fully reshape its hands-on core.

title: Fashion designers
rationale: Generative design, trend forecasting, virtual prototyping, CAD automation, and marketing tools can transform a large share of designers’ digital and creative workflow. Physical material selection, garment fitting, production oversight, brand judgment, and supplier collaboration still require substantial human expertise. Lower design costs will enable more collections, product variants, personalization, and small-label entry, but apparel consumption and manufacturing capacity limit demand expansion. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-enabled creative direction, curation, and technical execution rather than experience either wholesale replacement or proportionate job growth.

title: Film and video editors and camera operators
rationale: AI directly transforms editing through automated logging, rough cuts, reframing, color correction, effects, and generative footage, while robotic cameras and AI tracking reduce some routine camera work. Disruption is moderated because location shooting, live-event judgment, equipment handling, and collaboration with directors still require substantial human presence and creative control. Demand is highly elastic because lower production costs enable businesses, creators, and media organizations to produce far more video across streaming, advertising, social media, and internal communications. Thus, roles and workflows will change substantially, but expanding content volume should absorb much of the productivity gain, fitting the augment category.

title: Financial analysts
rationale: Financial analysis is predominantly digital and cognitive, and AI can already automate data gathering, financial-model construction, valuation comparisons, forecasting, monitoring, and report drafting. Human judgment, accountability, relationship management, and interpretation of unusual political or company-specific conditions will remain important, but analysts will oversee far more AI-generated work. Lower costs will expand analysis across more securities, scenarios, portfolios, and smaller organizations, although available capital, compliance requirements, and the limited need for duplicative investment opinions constrain demand growth. The combination of very high disruption and moderate demand elasticity therefore points to restructuring, with fewer routine junior tasks and greater emphasis on verification, differentiated insight, and stakeholder communication.

title: Financial clerks
rationale: Most financial-clerk tasks involve routine digital processing, including verifying records, calculating charges, preparing documents, updating accounts, and applying predetermined rules, making them highly amenable to AI and workflow automation. Customer communication and exception handling still require some human judgment, while gambling cage work retains a physical component, so disruption is not maximum. Demand is relatively inelastic because organizations need clerical processing mainly in proportion to underlying transactions, and making it cheaper is unlikely to generate enough additional billing, payroll, loan, or policy work to offset productivity gains. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to substantial headcount contraction and a replace outcome.

title: Financial examiners
rationale: Most core tasks—reviewing financial records, testing compliance, analyzing regulations, identifying anomalies, and drafting reports—are digital and increasingly automatable with AI. Human judgment, legal accountability, interviews, and onsite inspections remain important, especially for complex or contested findings. Cheaper examination could enable broader and more continuous oversight, but the number of regulated institutions and required examinations is largely determined by regulation rather than price. Therefore, AI is likely to reduce labor required per examination enough to constrain headcount despite growing compliance needs.

title: Financial managers
rationale: AI can substantially automate financial reporting, forecasting, compliance monitoring, cost analysis, and scenario modeling, materially changing this predominantly digital occupation. However, financial managers retain responsibility for supervision, executive advising, organization-specific judgment, regulatory accountability, and consequential capital and risk decisions. Lower-cost analysis may let organizations perform more frequent and sophisticated planning, but demand is constrained by the number and scale of organizations and managerial positions, so the occupation is likely to restructure around oversight, strategy, and AI-enabled decision-making rather than expand enough to qualify as augment.

title: Fire inspectors
rationale: AI can accelerate blueprint and code review, report preparation, evidence analysis, risk modeling, and remote wildfire monitoring. However, core duties still require onsite inspection, physical evidence collection, equipment testing, witness interviews, emergency response, and legally accountable human judgment. Demand may expand somewhat through more frequent inspections and proactive risk assessment, especially as wildfire threats grow, but statutory schedules, building stock, and government budgets constrain expansion. Because AI mainly improves supporting cognitive tasks rather than replacing fieldwork and enforcement authority, the occupation is resilient.

title: Firefighters
rationale: Core firefighting tasks require physical presence, strength, mobility, rapid judgment, and teamwork in dangerous, unpredictable environments that AI cannot readily replace. AI can improve dispatch, incident prediction, situational awareness, training, medical guidance, and report writing, but these remain supporting functions rather than substitutes for emergency crews. Demand is highly inelastic because communities will not consume substantially more emergency response when it becomes cheaper, while minimum staffing and readiness requirements also limit headcount reductions; therefore, the occupation is resilient.

title: Fishing and hunting workers
rationale: AI can improve fish detection, navigation, weather forecasting, catch optimization, and regulatory recordkeeping, but most core tasks remain physical, hazardous, and dependent on unpredictable outdoor conditions. Demand is highly inelastic because biological stocks, fishing quotas, hunting seasons, and catch limits constrain total output regardless of productivity or price. The occupation is therefore resilient to direct AI disruption, although continued mechanization and AI-assisted equipment may gradually reduce crew requirements.

title: Fitness trainers and instructors
rationale: AI can generate personalized workout plans, automate progress tracking, provide virtual instruction, and use computer vision or wearables to flag technique issues. However, live demonstration, nuanced safety supervision, emergency response, social accountability, and interpersonal motivation still favor an instructor’s physical presence. Lower-cost digital coaching could unlock substantial demand among people who cannot afford personal training, although participation time and motivation limit expansion. Because AI materially changes planning and monitoring but does not reshape most in-person instruction, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Flight attendants
rationale: Core duties require physical presence in an aircraft cabin, hands-on service, real-time passenger management, and decisive action during unpredictable safety or medical emergencies. AI may improve scheduling, translation, passenger communications, incident reporting, and risk monitoring, but it cannot readily replace the legally mandated onboard safety role. Demand is tied mainly to the number and size of flights, and lower-cost or faster task performance would not generate proportionally more air travel, especially because staffing minimums are regulated. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI affects peripheral tasks without substantially reshaping the core job.

title: Flooring installers and tile and stone setters
rationale: Core tasks are physical, site-specific, and dexterous, including surface preparation, cutting, positioning, fastening, grouting, and finishing in varied building environments. AI can improve estimating, measurement, layout visualization, material planning, scheduling, and customer service, but practical jobsite robotics are unlikely to replace most installation work within 10 years. Lower installation costs could stimulate some additional renovation and material upgrades, but demand remains constrained by construction activity, building stock, and how often floors need replacement. The low disruption score therefore makes the occupation resilient despite limited potential for demand expansion.

title: Floral designers
rationale: The core work is hands-on: selecting, cutting, arranging, preserving, transporting, and installing fragile, variable plant materials in physical settings. AI can assist with design concepts, customer visualization, order taking, pricing, inventory, and marketing, but automating production would require capable robotics that is unlikely to be economical for many small shops. Lower design labor costs could modestly increase purchases of custom arrangements and recurring decor, but demand remains constrained by occasions, perishable-material costs, and delivery logistics. Because AI mainly improves peripheral cognitive and administrative tasks rather than replacing physical floral craft, the occupation is resilient.

title: Food and beverage serving and related workers
rationale: AI-enabled kiosks, voice ordering, reservation systems, and automated payments can substantially change customer-facing transaction tasks, especially in fast-food and counter service. However, preparing and carrying food, cleaning, stocking, setting tables, and responding to unpredictable physical situations still require on-site labor, while robotics remains costly and operationally constrained. Cheaper service could shift some meals from home preparation to restaurants, but demand is limited by food consumption, dining time, and establishment capacity. The occupation is therefore resilient overall, although staffing and task mixes may change in highly standardized venues.

title: Food preparation workers
rationale: Core tasks involve dexterous physical work in crowded, variable kitchens, including cutting ingredients, cleaning equipment, moving supplies, and maintaining food safety. AI may improve scheduling, inventory management, instructions, and temperature monitoring, while specialized machinery and preprocessed ingredients can automate some repetitive preparation, but capable general-purpose kitchen robotics remain limited. Demand is relatively inelastic because food consumption is bounded, although lower preparation costs could modestly increase purchases of prepared meals. The occupation is therefore resilient to AI specifically, even as conventional automation and operational changes may gradually reduce employment.

title: Food processing equipment workers
rationale: Core duties require physical presence to load ingredients, set up and clean machinery, inspect products, and respond to equipment or process problems in a demanding production environment. AI-enabled sensors, computer vision, predictive maintenance, and automated process controls will reduce routine monitoring and recordkeeping, but deploying systems that handle variable ingredients and sanitation requirements will be gradual. Demand is relatively inelastic because consumers will not eat dramatically more food if processing becomes cheaper, so productivity gains may reduce staffing per production line. Nevertheless, the occupation is resilient because AI mainly improves or automates portions of machine tending rather than replacing the hands-on core of the job.

title: Food service managers
rationale: AI can substantially assist with scheduling, inventory forecasting, purchasing, payroll, budgeting, compliance documentation, and performance monitoring. However, the core role still requires on-site leadership, real-time coordination, safety oversight, customer conflict resolution, and hands-on responses to unpredictable operational problems. Demand for managers is tied mainly to the number and scale of food establishments, so productivity gains are more likely to let each manager oversee more operations than to create much more demand. Because AI changes administrative work but does not displace the physical and interpersonal core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Forensic science technicians
rationale: AI will materially improve image and pattern matching, DNA-result interpretation, statistical analysis, report drafting, and crime-scene reconstruction. However, evidence collection, laboratory procedures, chain-of-custody compliance, equipment handling, expert judgment, and courtroom testimony still require substantial human presence and accountability. Demand may expand through reduced backlogs, cold-case reviews, and more evidence analyzed per case, but crime volumes, public budgets, and legal procedures impose strong limits. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI significantly assists its analytical components without reshaping most of its hands-on and legally accountable core.

title: Forest and conservation workers
rationale: Core duties such as planting, brush clearing, tree removal, equipment maintenance, and wildfire suppression are strenuous physical tasks in remote, unpredictable environments, placing them largely beyond AI’s direct reach. AI-enabled remote sensing, mapping, and species or disease identification can reduce time spent surveying forests and planning fieldwork, but these are limited portions of the job. Cheaper work could support additional restoration, wildfire mitigation, and land maintenance, although government budgets, land availability, and seasonal constraints limit expansion. Because AI primarily improves peripheral monitoring and coordination rather than replacing field execution, the occupation is resilient.

title: Fundraisers
rationale: AI can substantially automate donor research, prospect scoring, message drafting, campaign personalization, compliance checks, recordkeeping, and performance analysis. However, cultivating trust with major donors, negotiating gifts, managing volunteers, and representing organizations at events remain strongly human and relationship-based. Lower campaign costs should let nonprofits conduct more outreach and pursue smaller donor segments, but charitable budgets and the finite supply of donors limit headcount expansion. The occupation therefore will persist, while shifting toward relationship management, strategy, and AI-enabled campaign oversight.

title: Funeral service workers
rationale: AI can substantially streamline paperwork, scheduling, obituary drafting, benefits applications, marketing, and routine client communications. However, preparing and transporting remains, coordinating ceremonies, managing facilities, and compassionately guiding grieving families require hands-on presence, judgment, and trust. Demand is largely fixed by mortality and demographic trends, so cheaper services would not generate many more funerals, although preplanning could expand modestly. Because AI changes administrative portions rather than the occupation’s physical and interpersonal core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Gambling services workers
rationale: Most workers, especially dealers and floor supervisors, perform in-person tasks involving physical game operation, customer interaction, rule enforcement, and real-time judgment, limiting direct AI substitution. AI and automation can still streamline bet processing, payouts, surveillance, scheduling, and administrative work, while online gambling particularly reduces demand for sportsbook writers and runners. Overall gambling demand is constrained by regulation, consumer spending, and market saturation, so cheaper operations are unlikely to produce enough additional play to offset automation fully. Because disruption remains moderate for the occupation's large in-person workforce, the aggregate occupation is resilient despite contraction in its more transactional roles.

title: General maintenance and repair workers
rationale: Most core tasks require physical presence, dexterity, tool use, and adaptation to varied buildings and machinery, keeping direct AI disruption low. AI can improve diagnostics, preventive-maintenance scheduling, parts ordering, estimates, recordkeeping, and access to repair instructions, but workers must still perform the repairs. Lower costs may unlock some deferred maintenance and more preventive work, although demand remains constrained by the installed stock of buildings and equipment. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI primarily improving worker productivity rather than replacing the hands-on role.

title: General office clerks
rationale: Most core duties—data entry, document preparation, scheduling, record management, billing, and routine communications—are directly automatable with current AI and workflow software. In-person reception and handling physical mail provide some residual need, preventing a maximum disruption score. Demand for clerical processing is largely tied to a fixed volume of organizational transactions, so lower costs are unlikely to generate enough additional work to offset productivity gains, making significant headcount replacement likely.

title: Genetic counselors
rationale: AI can substantially automate pedigree analysis, variant interpretation support, risk calculations, literature review, patient education, and clinical documentation. However, communicating uncertain or distressing results, supporting consequential decisions, and assuming clinical responsibility still require licensed professionals with empathy and contextual judgment. Cheaper delivery should unlock meaningful demand as genetic testing expands, but testing volumes, reimbursement, regulation, and the episodic nature of counseling limit expansion. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity therefore points to restructuring around AI-assisted analysis and more complex, human-centered counseling.

title: Geographers
rationale: Most geographic analysis is digital and data-intensive, including GIS processing, remote-sensing interpretation, mapping, statistical analysis, visualization, and report writing, all of which AI can substantially accelerate. Field observations, interviews, methodological judgment, and stakeholder communication remain important human tasks, preventing near-total automation. Cheaper geographic analysis could expand its use in planning, climate adaptation, logistics, and risk assessment, but government budgets and the finite number of major planning decisions limit demand growth. High disruption combined with moderate elasticity therefore points to restructuring, with greater emphasis on problem framing, validation, domain expertise, and oversight of AI-enabled geospatial workflows.

title: Geological and hydrologic technicians
rationale: AI can substantially assist with data cleaning, sample interpretation, GIS mapping, modeling, and report preparation, especially for office-based technicians. However, collecting physical samples, installing and maintaining instruments, conducting laboratory procedures, and operating in remote or unpredictable environments still require substantial human presence. Lower costs could support denser environmental monitoring and more resource analysis, but demand remains constrained by project activity, regulation, commodity markets, and government funding. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI reshapes its analytical components without displacing most of its field and laboratory core.

title: Geoscientists
rationale: AI will materially accelerate remote-sensing interpretation, GIS analysis, geological modeling, deposit estimation, mapping, and report preparation. However, field surveys, sample collection, laboratory work, site-specific judgment, client coordination, and licensed professional accountability still require substantial human involvement. Lower analysis costs could expand environmental assessments, hazard mapping, and resource exploration, but demand remains constrained by fieldwork, regulation, and the number of viable development projects. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI substantially enhances its analytical components without fully reshaping its mixed field-and-office core.

title: Glaziers
rationale: Glaziers perform predominantly physical, site-specific work involving heavy and fragile materials, precise fitting, work at heights, and adaptation to variable building conditions. AI may assist with blueprint interpretation, measurements, estimating, scheduling, and safety planning, but current robotics cannot economically handle most field installation tasks. Cheaper and faster installation could stimulate some additional renovation and architectural-glass demand, although construction volumes, material costs, and replacement cycles limit expansion. The low disruption score therefore makes the occupation resilient over the next decade.

title: Graphic designers
rationale: Graphic design is predominantly digital, and generative AI can already produce concepts, illustrations, layouts, variations, and routine revisions, placing nearly all production tasks in AI’s direct path. Cheaper design will increase visual-content demand, especially among small businesses and for personalized digital marketing, but self-service tools and finite branding budgets limit how much of that expansion becomes demand for professional designers. Human value will shift toward art direction, brand strategy, client interpretation, quality control, and distinctive creative judgment. High disruption combined with moderate demand elasticity therefore points to restructuring rather than broad replacement or assured employment growth.

title: Grounds maintenance workers
rationale: Core tasks are physical, site-specific, and performed in variable outdoor environments using tools and heavy equipment, putting most of the occupation beyond near-term AI capabilities. AI can improve scheduling, plant-health diagnosis, landscape planning, and routing, while autonomous mowers and sprayers may automate some standardized work, but planting, pruning, cleanup, repairs, and tree work still require human dexterity and judgment. Lower costs could moderately expand demand for professional lawn care, landscaping, and urban green-space maintenance, although available land and customers' desired maintenance frequency impose limits. Because disruption remains low despite some equipment automation, the occupation is resilient.

title: Hand laborers and material movers
rationale: Core tasks involve physically lifting, sorting, packing, cleaning, and moving varied objects in real-world environments, so current AI mainly improves routing, inventory tracking, scheduling, and instructions. Robotics enhanced by AI will automate some structured warehouse, feeding, and packaging tasks, but deployment costs and difficulty handling irregular environments limit occupation-wide disruption over the next decade. Cheaper material handling may support more e-commerce and logistics activity, but demand remains tied to the volume of physical goods, waste, and vehicles rather than expanding proportionally with productivity. Therefore, AI will change workflows and reduce some specialized roles, but the broad occupation remains resilient.

title: Hazardous materials removal workers
rationale: Core duties involve strenuous, hands-on work in hazardous, confined, and unpredictable environments, so AI will mainly assist with monitoring, material identification, compliance documentation, training, and site planning. Cheaper remediation could unlock cleanup at some deferred contaminated sites, but demand remains constrained by the finite stock of hazardous material, regulation, construction activity, and public or private funding. Because AI is unlikely to replace the occupation's physical onsite work over the next decade, the occupation is resilient despite modest changes to its administrative and decision-support tasks.

title: Health and safety engineers
rationale: AI will materially assist with regulatory analysis, plan review, risk modeling, sensor-data interpretation, incident documentation, and safety-program design. However, site inspections, contextual hazard recognition, worker interviews, corrective-action implementation, and professional accountability still require substantial human judgment and real-world presence. Lower costs could encourage more frequent assessments and continuous monitoring, but demand remains partly constrained by the number of facilities, projects, and compliance requirements. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI reshapes its analytical workflow without taking over its core field-based responsibilities.

title: Health education specialists
rationale: AI can substantially accelerate needs assessment, data analysis, educational-material creation, program design, grant writing, and evaluation, although community engagement, instruction, trust building, and stakeholder coordination still require people. Cheaper, more personalized health education could expand preventive-health programs, but government and nonprofit budgets, institutional constraints, and the need for human outreach limit headcount growth. The occupation therefore faces substantial changes in workflows and required skills, while moderate demand expansion should prevent wholesale replacement.

title: Health information technologists and medical registrars
rationale: The occupation is predominantly computer-based, and AI can increasingly automate record abstraction, classification, data-quality checks, database updates, report generation, and portions of clinical analysis. Human expertise will remain important for system implementation, ambiguous records, regulatory compliance, privacy oversight, and coordination with healthcare staff. Lower costs will enable more analysis of rapidly growing health data, but demand is constrained by healthcare budgets, mandated registry workloads, and the finite number of provider organizations. High disruption combined with moderate demand elasticity therefore points to restructuring, with fewer routine registry tasks and greater emphasis on governance, validation, systems integration, and advanced analytics.

title: Heating, air conditioning, and refrigeration mechanics and installers
rationale: HVAC work is dominated by on-site installation, inspection, repair, wiring, refrigerant handling, and work in cramped or unpredictable physical environments, which AI cannot readily perform. AI-enabled diagnostics, sensor analysis, load calculations, scheduling, customer communication, and recordkeeping will improve productivity, but these tools affect only part of the technician’s job. Lower service costs could encourage more preventive maintenance, retrofits, and energy-efficiency upgrades, although demand remains constrained by the building stock and equipment replacement cycles, so the occupation is resilient.

title: Heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers
rationale: Autonomous-driving systems directly target the occupation’s central task, especially repetitive highway travel, while AI already supports routing, safety monitoring, dispatch, and compliance. Complex urban driving, adverse weather, cargo handling, inspections, liability rules, and specialized loads will slow full automation, but hub-to-hub autonomy could eliminate substantial long-haul driving hours within a decade. Freight demand may rise somewhat as transportation costs fall, but it is ultimately constrained by demand for physical goods, so expansion is unlikely to offset large productivity gains and the net effect is replacement.

title: Heavy vehicle and mobile equipment service technicians
rationale: The occupation is dominated by hands-on inspection, disassembly, repair, welding, parts replacement, and fieldwork on large machines in varied physical environments. AI will improve fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, manual lookup, calibration guidance, and recordkeeping, but technicians must still manipulate heavy components and respond to unpredictable equipment conditions. Cheaper, faster service could encourage more preventive maintenance and reduce equipment downtime, although demand remains constrained by the installed fleet and actual wear rates. Because AI primarily assists troubleshooting rather than replacing physical repair work, the occupation is resilient.

title: High school teachers
rationale: AI will materially accelerate lesson planning, grading, assessment design, differentiation, parent communications, and routine content delivery. However, classroom management, student motivation, safeguarding, supervision, and relationship-based instruction still require sustained human presence, keeping disruption below the high range. Demand is constrained by enrollment, public budgets, licensing rules, and practical class-size requirements, so cheaper instructional preparation would generate only limited additional teacher demand. The occupation is therefore resilient, although teachers’ workflows and expected AI skills will change substantially.

title: Historians
rationale: Historical research is predominantly cognitive and language-based, and AI can already search digitized collections, summarize sources, translate texts, identify patterns, and draft reports or exhibits. Human expertise remains important for source authentication, original interpretation, physical artifacts, archival fieldwork, and public engagement, preventing maximum disruption. Demand may expand through digitization and cheaper historical content, but historian employment is constrained by limited government, museum, and nonprofit funding. With high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains are likely to reduce staffing needs and concentrate work among fewer historians.

title: Home health and personal care aides
rationale: Core duties such as bathing, dressing, lifting, meal preparation, transportation, and responding to changing conditions require hands-on presence in unpredictable home environments. AI can improve scheduling, documentation, remote monitoring, care plans, and alerts, but current robotics cannot broadly replace intimate physical care or human companionship. Demand is highly responsive because aging, caregiver shortages, and affordability constraints create substantial unmet need, although care needs and public reimbursement limit unlimited expansion. With disruption below 7, the occupation remains resilient and AI primarily supports aides rather than replacing them.

title: Human resources managers
rationale: AI can substantially automate recruiting workflows, policy drafting, compliance monitoring, workforce analytics, benefits administration, and routine employee communications. Sensitive investigations, dispute mediation, executive advising, negotiation, and accountability still require human judgment and trust, preventing an even higher disruption score. Organizations are unlikely to demand proportionally more HR management when these functions become cheaper, although expanding regulation and talent-management needs create some additional demand. As AI enables each manager to oversee broader operations with fewer specialists and support staff, the occupation faces gradual headcount compression and consolidation.

title: Human resources specialists
rationale: Most HR specialist work is digital, language-based, and highly exposed to AI, including candidate sourcing and screening, interview support, policy guidance, recordkeeping, onboarding, and routine compliance documentation. Human judgment, sensitive employee relations, organizational context, and legal accountability will preserve some roles, but AI can substantially reduce the time required for core workflows. Demand may expand modestly as smaller employers gain access to better HR services, yet hiring volume and employee populations impose structural limits, so productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount and shift remaining positions toward complex advisory work.

title: Hydrologists
rationale: AI can materially accelerate hydrologic modeling, remote-sensing analysis, forecasting, literature review, and report preparation, which constitute a large share of the occupation's knowledge work. Field sampling, site-specific judgment, stakeholder collaboration, and responsibility for consequential water-management decisions will continue to require human experts. Cheaper analysis should enable more frequent and geographically detailed assessments amid growing flood, drought, contamination, and water-supply risks, but government budgets, regulation, and the pace of infrastructure projects limit demand expansion. The result is restructuring: fewer hours per analysis and greater emphasis on field validation, model oversight, interdisciplinary interpretation, and decision support.

title: Industrial designers
rationale: Generative design, AI-assisted CAD, simulation, rendering, market research, and rapid concept generation can materially accelerate much of the occupation’s digital workflow. However, physical prototyping, manufacturing knowledge, safety and usability evaluation, client judgment, and cross-functional coordination remain important human responsibilities. Lower design costs should enable smaller firms, more product variants, and faster iteration, but demand is constrained by manufacturing costs and the limited need for additional physical products. The result is substantial restructuring toward AI-enabled direction, validation, and engineering integration rather than wholesale replacement.

title: Industrial engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: AI can substantially accelerate statistical analysis, cost modeling, scheduling, CAD documentation, and workflow optimization, changing a large share of the occupation's knowledge tasks. However, technicians must still collect reliable shop-floor data, observe workers and machinery, test processes, and coordinate changes at manufacturing sites, limiting end-to-end automation. Cheaper analysis may encourage more continuous process improvement and support greater automation, but demand remains constrained by the number of facilities, production lines, and capital projects. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient, although its work will become more AI-enabled and analytically focused.

title: Industrial engineers
rationale: AI can materially accelerate process-data analysis, simulation, optimization, system design, documentation, and presentation work, placing much of the occupation's cognitive core in its path. However, observing physical operations, diagnosing context-specific problems, validating safety and quality, and securing organizational buy-in still require engineers on site and working with people. Lower costs could broaden access to industrial-engineering services and support more automation and supply-chain projects, but physical investment cycles and implementation constraints limit demand expansion. The occupation therefore is likely to persist with substantially changed tools and skills rather than experience either wholesale replacement or enough growth to absorb all productivity gains.

title: Industrial machinery mechanics, machinery maintenance workers, and millwrights
rationale: The occupation is dominated by hands-on, site-specific work such as inspecting, disassembling, repairing, aligning, welding, and moving heavy machinery. AI-powered diagnostics, predictive maintenance, technical-manual assistants, and scheduling tools will improve troubleshooting and reduce routine inspections, but they cannot readily perform physical repairs in varied industrial environments. Demand has moderate elasticity because cheaper maintenance and expanding industrial automation will increase the amount of machinery installed and serviced, although maintenance needs remain constrained by the installed equipment base. With disruption below the high-disruption threshold, the occupation is resilient, even as workers increasingly use AI-enabled diagnostic tools.

title: Industrial production managers
rationale: AI will materially improve production scheduling, forecasting, quality monitoring, report generation, and root-cause analysis, changing a substantial share of managers’ analytical work. However, plant-floor presence, personnel leadership, safety accountability, cross-functional negotiation, and responses to physical emergencies remain difficult to automate. Demand for these managers is tied mainly to the number and complexity of production facilities, so greater productivity is more likely to widen managerial spans than generate proportionally more positions. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient despite relatively inelastic demand.

title: Information clerks
rationale: Most core tasks—data collection, record maintenance, routine correspondence, eligibility screening, reservations, and answering standard questions—are structured digital or language activities increasingly handled by AI and self-service systems. Human presence remains useful for unusual cases, sensitive interactions, regulatory accountability, front-desk service, and some physical duties, preventing a maximum disruption score. Demand is relatively inelastic because organizations need only a finite number of records, bookings, applications, and customer inquiries processed; making these tasks cheaper will not generate proportionally more work. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount contraction and a net effect of replace.

title: Information security analysts
rationale: The occupation is almost entirely digital and cognitive, and AI can already automate alert triage, threat intelligence synthesis, vulnerability discovery, report generation, and parts of incident investigation. Human analysts will remain important for adversarial reasoning, novel attacks, organizational judgment, accountability, and coordinating incident response, but their workflows and required skills will change substantially. Demand is highly elastic because many organizations remain underprotected, attack surfaces are expanding, and cheaper analysis enables more continuous monitoring, testing, and security coverage. These factors make augmentation most likely: analysts will secure more systems with AI while growing cyber risk absorbs much of the productivity gain.

title: Instructional coordinators
rationale: AI can substantially automate curriculum drafting, standards alignment, test-data analysis, material review, and the preparation of training resources. Classroom observation, teacher coaching, institutional judgment, and stakeholder buy-in still require experienced human involvement, preventing a higher disruption score. Demand may expand through greater curriculum personalization and more frequent evaluation, but fixed school populations, regulation, and tight public-sector budgets limit that expansion. With high disruption and low elasticity, productivity gains are likely to reduce coordinator headcount while concentrating remaining roles on implementation, mentoring, and governance.

title: Insulation workers
rationale: Core tasks involve physically removing, cutting, fitting, spraying, and securing materials in cramped, hazardous, and highly variable worksites, making them difficult for AI or near-term robotics to automate. AI can assist with blueprint review, material estimation, scheduling, safety training, and documentation, but these are peripheral to installation work. Lower installation costs could meaningfully increase energy-efficiency retrofits and insulation upgrades, although demand remains constrained by the building stock, construction activity, and material costs. Because AI is unlikely to reshape the occupation's hands-on core over the next decade, the occupation is resilient.

title: Insurance sales agents
rationale: Most core tasks—including prospecting, needs analysis, policy comparison, explanations, renewals, claims assistance, and recordkeeping—are language- and data-based and increasingly automatable through AI agents and digital sales platforms. Human trust, persuasion, licensing accountability, and guidance for complex commercial or financial products will preserve a role for experienced agents, but substantially fewer may handle a larger client base. Demand could expand somewhat as cheaper advice reaches underserved customers, yet insurance purchases remain constrained by risk exposure, regulation, and household or business budgets. High disruption combined with limited demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount contraction and a shift toward complex, relationship-intensive sales.

title: Insurance underwriters
rationale: Underwriting is predominantly digital, rules-based analytical work, and automated systems already screen applicants, estimate risk, recommend prices, and handle many routine decisions. More capable AI can process unstructured records and explain exceptions, leaving humans concentrated in complex commercial risks, regulatory oversight, and relationship management. Cheaper underwriting may modestly expand coverage and enable more customized policies, but insurance demand is constrained by underlying exposure, customer budgets, regulation, and insurers’ risk capacity. With very high disruption and low demand elasticity, productivity gains are likely to reduce headcount rather than generate enough additional underwriting work to compensate.

title: Interior designers
rationale: Generative design, visualization, CAD/BIM automation, product selection, cost estimation, and code-checking can materially accelerate a large share of designers’ cognitive and digital work. However, client discovery, site assessment, contractor coordination, installation oversight, and accountability for practical constraints still require substantial human involvement. Lower design costs could unlock demand among households and small businesses that currently forgo professional services, but construction costs and the finite number of renovation projects limit expansion, making substantial skill restructuring more likely than either wholesale replacement or fully compensating growth.

title: Interpreters and translators
rationale: Written translation and much spoken interpretation are language-based tasks directly exposed to rapidly improving machine translation, speech recognition, and voice-generation systems. Human expertise will remain important for high-stakes legal, medical, diplomatic, literary, and sign-language work, but many workers will shift from producing first drafts to supervising, post-editing, and validating AI output. Lower costs will substantially increase translated and localized content, although not enough to preserve all routine translation and interpretation roles. The occupation therefore faces major skill and workflow changes, with specialists and AI-adapted workers faring better than generalists.

title: Ironworkers
rationale: Ironworking is dominated by physical, safety-critical tasks performed at changing outdoor jobsites, including rigging, positioning, welding, bolting, and tying steel. AI can improve blueprint interpretation, layout, scheduling, safety monitoring, and equipment guidance, but autonomous robots are unlikely to handle most unstructured, high-altitude fieldwork within the next decade. Cheaper ironworking could enable some additional construction and infrastructure rehabilitation, but demand remains constrained by financing, land, permitting, material costs, and fixed project needs, so the occupation is resilient.

title: Janitors and building cleaners
rationale: Most core duties require physical presence, mobility, manual handling, and adaptation to varied buildings, spills, repairs, and safety hazards. AI may improve scheduling, supply management, building monitoring, and robotic floor cleaning, but general-purpose cleaning robots are unlikely to automate most tasks within the next decade. Lower costs could support somewhat more frequent cleaning, although demand remains constrained by building area, occupancy, and sanitation budgets. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI primarily changes equipment and peripheral tasks rather than replacing the core hands-on work.

title: Jewelers and precious stone and metal workers
rationale: AI can accelerate CAD design, cost estimation, gemstone imaging, appraisal research, marketing, and customer visualization, while 3D printing and robotic polishing further automate standardized production. However, much of the occupation still requires dexterous manipulation of valuable materials, close visual inspection, repairs to unique objects, stone setting, and trusted customer interaction. Lower design and production costs may stimulate customization and increase output somewhat, but demand is constrained by discretionary spending, material costs, imports, and the limited frequency of jewelry purchases. Because disruption remains moderate and the hands-on core persists, the occupation is resilient even though automation may contribute to gradual employment decline.

title: Judges and hearing officers
rationale: Much of the occupation consists of language-intensive knowledge work—legal research, record review, evidence synthesis, precedent comparison, and drafting decisions—that AI can substantially accelerate. Presiding over contentious proceedings, assessing credibility, exercising discretion, and providing legitimate human accountability remain important barriers to full automation, keeping disruption at the low end of high. Demand is constrained by case volumes, government budgets, authorized judgeships, and procedural rules, so faster adjudication is unlikely to produce proportionate employment growth. With high disruption and low elasticity, AI is likely to reduce staffing needs, especially for routine administrative adjudication, even while human judges retain final authority.

title: Kindergarten and elementary school teachers
rationale: AI can materially streamline lesson planning, grading, assessment, parent communications, and creation of personalized instructional materials. However, classroom instruction, child supervision, behavior management, motivation, and social-emotional development require sustained human presence and judgment, limiting disruption of the occupation’s core. Demand is tied primarily to student enrollment, class-size policies, licensing rules, and public budgets, so greater teacher productivity is unlikely to generate proportionally more teaching positions. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient, although teachers’ workflows and supporting skills will change substantially.

title: Labor relations specialists
rationale: AI can substantially automate contract and policy drafting, agreement comparison, compliance research, grievance triage, case summarization, and training-material preparation. Human specialists will remain important for sensitive investigations, tense negotiations, relationship building, and accountable judgment, but AI will reduce the labor required around these interpersonal tasks. Demand is constrained by the number of unionized workplaces, negotiations, and disputes rather than by the cost of specialist analysis, so cheaper service is unlikely to generate proportionate new work; high disruption combined with low elasticity therefore points to headcount contraction.

title: Landscape architects
rationale: AI-enabled CADD, GIS analysis, generative design, visualization, cost estimation, and document production will materially accelerate a large share of landscape architects’ office-based work. However, client negotiation, site inspection, local ecological judgment, multidisciplinary coordination, and licensed responsibility still require substantial human involvement. Lower design costs could expand demand among smaller developments, homeowners, and climate-resilience projects, but demand remains constrained by construction activity, land availability, regulation, and project budgets. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-assisted design and higher-level judgment rather than experience wholesale replacement.

title: Lawyers
rationale: Legal research, document review, drafting, contract analysis, and case preparation are predominantly language-based tasks that AI can already accelerate substantially. Advocacy, negotiation, client trust, professional judgment, and licensed representation preserve an important human role, but they do not shield much of the occupation’s underlying workload. Lower prices will unlock some unmet demand for legal help, especially among individuals and small businesses, yet courts, licensing rules, budgets, and the finite number of disputes and transactions limit expansion. With very high disruption and low demand elasticity, productivity gains are likely to reduce lawyer hours and headcount relative to the amount of legal work performed.

title: Librarians and library media specialists
rationale: AI directly affects core knowledge tasks such as reference research, cataloging, search-result evaluation, collection recommendations, instructional preparation, and routine administration. In-person teaching, community programming, patron support, and stewardship of physical collections remain human-centered, preventing an even higher disruption score. Demand is constrained by public and school budgets, institutional staffing models, and a finite number of libraries, so cheaper information services are unlikely to expand enough to offset productivity-driven staffing reductions.

title: Library technicians and assistants
rationale: AI can automate routine reference responses, cataloging, database maintenance, clerical work, and some patron instruction, while self-service systems further reduce circulation duties. However, reshelving and processing physical materials, assisting patrons in person, and running community programs still require substantial on-site human presence. Demand is relatively inelastic because library staffing is constrained by public and educational budgets, and cheaper service is unlikely to produce proportionately more library use. The disruption score remains just below the high threshold because of the occupation's physical and interpersonal core, so it is categorized as resilient despite likely gradual headcount decline.

title: Licensed practical and licensed vocational nurses
rationale: AI can streamline documentation, care-plan updates, patient monitoring, risk alerts, and communication, materially changing the administrative portion of LPN/LVN work. However, core duties such as bathing, dressing, wound care, medication administration, specimen collection, and bedside observation require licensed human presence, physical dexterity, and interpersonal judgment. Demand will rise with population aging and chronic illness, but it is constrained by patients’ actual care needs, reimbursement, regulation, and facility capacity, so cheaper delivery would not produce proportionate growth. Because disruption remains moderate rather than high, the occupation is resilient despite meaningful workflow augmentation.

title: Loan officers
rationale: Most underwriting, document verification, compliance review, product explanation, and routine applicant communication are digital tasks already supported by automated decision systems and increasingly addressable by AI. Human relationship-building, sales, exception handling, and complex commercial-loan structuring remain important, but they represent a smaller share of many consumer and mortgage workflows. Cheaper processing may modestly expand access to credit, yet demand is constrained by interest rates, borrower creditworthiness, capital availability, regulation, and underlying financing needs, so expansion is unlikely to offset large productivity gains. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount pressure and a replace net effect.

title: Lodging managers
rationale: AI will materially improve revenue management, forecasting, scheduling, budgeting, guest communications, and administrative reporting. However, the occupation still depends heavily on physical inspections, staff leadership, interpersonal conflict resolution, and handling unpredictable on-site guest and facility problems. Demand is relatively inelastic because the number of managers is tied mainly to the number, size, and complexity of lodging properties rather than the cost of managerial analysis. With disruption remaining moderate, the occupation is resilient, although AI may enable some managers to oversee larger operations or multiple properties.

title: Logging workers
rationale: Logging is predominantly physical, site-specific work involving heavy machinery, hazardous terrain, and rapid real-world judgment, so AI will mainly assist rather than perform most core tasks. Computer vision, equipment monitoring, route planning, automated grading, and increasingly autonomous harvesters may improve productivity, especially for equipment operators and log graders. Demand is relatively inelastic because timber consumption is constrained by construction and manufacturing needs, although cheaper harvesting and forest-thinning programs could create modest additional work. Because disruption remains low over the next decade, the occupation is resilient even as continued mechanization gradually reduces headcount.

title: Logisticians
rationale: Forecasting, inventory allocation, route planning, risk monitoring, and supply-chain analysis are predominantly digital tasks that AI and optimization systems can substantially automate. Human logisticians will remain important for managing disruptions, negotiating with suppliers, implementing systems, and coordinating decisions across organizations and physical facilities. Lower-cost logistics analysis will support more frequent optimization and help firms manage increasingly complex, resilient supply chains, but demand remains constrained by the volume of physical commerce. The occupation therefore will be restructured around exception handling, strategic judgment, relationships, and AI-system oversight rather than eliminated.

title: Machinists and tool and die makers
rationale: AI-enabled CAM programming, machine vision, predictive maintenance, and automated process optimization will materially reduce time spent interpreting designs, selecting toolpaths, and inspecting parts. However, physical setup, workholding, calibration, manual finishing, troubleshooting, and safe operation in varied shop conditions still require skilled on-site workers. Lower machining costs may expand demand for customized and small-batch parts, but demand remains constrained by broader manufacturing volumes and capital equipment, so the occupation is resilient even as automation changes parts of the workflow.

title: Management analysts
rationale: AI directly affects most analytical tasks, including gathering information, analyzing financial and operational data, developing alternatives, and drafting reports, proposals, and presentations. Human analysts remain important for diagnosing ambiguous organizational problems, interviewing stakeholders, exercising industry judgment, building trust, and managing implementation. Cheaper consulting could unlock substantial demand among smaller organizations and enable more frequent analysis, but adoption is limited by management attention, implementation capacity, and the value clients place on accountable human advice. The occupation therefore will persist, but its skill mix and staffing model will shift substantially toward AI-enabled analysis, stakeholder management, and change execution.

title: Manicurists and pedicurists
rationale: Core services require precise physical manipulation of each client’s hands and feet, safe use of sharp tools and chemicals, sanitation, creativity, and in-person customer interaction. AI can assist with scheduling, marketing, inventory, design visualization, and business administration, but robotics is unlikely to handle the full treatment safely and economically within the next decade. If services became much faster and cheaper, customers could purchase them more frequently and broader income groups could participate, although grooming cycles and the need for in-person appointments limit expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI primarily improves peripheral tasks rather than reshaping its hands-on core.

title: Marine engineers and naval architects
rationale: AI-enabled generative design, simulation, optimization, drafting, cost estimation, and technical reporting will materially accelerate a large share of this occupation’s knowledge work. However, engineers will remain responsible for safety-critical judgment, regulatory compliance, interdisciplinary coordination, and physical construction and testing in demanding real-world environments. Lower design costs should support more design iterations and some additional vessel, offshore-energy, and coastal-infrastructure projects, but demand is constrained by high construction costs, long project cycles, and limited shipbuilding volume. The result is restructuring: fewer hours devoted to routine analysis and documentation, with greater emphasis on systems integration, validation, oversight, and accountability.

title: Market research analysts
rationale: Nearly all core tasks—data gathering, statistical analysis, trend forecasting, visualization, report writing, and competitive research—are digital and increasingly automatable with AI. Cheaper analysis will enable more frequent studies, finer customer segmentation, and greater adoption by smaller businesses, but demand remains constrained by marketing budgets, available data, and the finite number of consequential business decisions. The occupation will therefore restructure around research design, validation, domain judgment, stakeholder communication, and translating automated findings into strategy, while fewer workers may be needed for routine analysis and reporting.

title: Marriage and family therapists
rationale: Therapy is predominantly conversational and cognitive, placing assessment, treatment planning, documentation, and routine client support directly in AI’s path. However, licensure, clinical accountability, therapeutic trust, crisis judgment, and nuanced management of couples and families preserve an important human role. Demand is highly elastic because cost, provider shortages, scheduling, and stigma currently leave substantial mental-health needs unmet. AI-enabled productivity should therefore expand access and caseload capacity while substantially changing therapists’ workflows, making augment the best fit.

title: Masonry workers
rationale: Core masonry tasks require dexterity, strength, visual judgment, and physical presence in variable and often hazardous jobsite conditions, placing them largely beyond near-term AI capabilities. AI can assist with blueprint interpretation, material estimates, layout, scheduling, and quality monitoring, while robotics may automate portions of standardized bricklaying or concrete finishing, but these applications will remain limited. Dramatically lower labor costs could encourage more masonry construction and substitution away from other materials, although demand would still be constrained by overall construction activity, land, materials, and project budgets. Because AI mainly affects peripheral planning tasks rather than the hands-on core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Massage therapists
rationale: The occupation’s core work is hands-on manipulation requiring physical strength, tactile feedback, real-time adaptation, trust, and in-person interaction, all of which remain difficult for AI or robotics to reproduce economically. AI can assist with scheduling, marketing, documentation, intake, and treatment suggestions, but these are peripheral to delivering a massage. Lower prices could unlock meaningful additional demand for pain relief, stress reduction, and wellness services, although session time, consumer preferences, and practical limits on treatment frequency constrain expansion. Because disruption remains low despite moderate demand elasticity, the occupation is resilient.

title: Material moving machine operators
rationale: Autonomous forklifts, robotic material-handling systems, machine vision, and AI-based routing can increasingly perform the repetitive movement and monitoring tasks common in structured warehouses and factories. Adoption will be slower for cranes, dredges, construction sites, and irregular facilities because these environments require situational judgment, safety coordination, and hands-on inspection or repair. Demand for material movement rises with e-commerce and production, but it is fundamentally tied to physical shipment volumes, so cheaper operation is unlikely to generate enough additional work to offset large productivity gains, making replacement the best fit.

title: Material recording clerks
rationale: Much of the occupation consists of routine recordkeeping, inventory reconciliation, reporting, scheduling, and vendor communication that AI-enabled software can automate. RFID, sensors, computer vision, and warehouse-management systems can also reduce manual counting and inspection, although package handling and resolving physical exceptions still require on-site workers. Demand for clerks is tied mainly to the volume of goods moving through supply chains, so cheaper clerical processing is unlikely to create proportionate new demand. High disruption combined with inelastic demand points to replacement and substantial headcount contraction.

title: Materials engineers
rationale: AI will substantially accelerate materials-property prediction, candidate screening, simulation, optimization, data analysis, and technical reporting. However, core responsibilities still require laboratory experiments, physical failure investigation, manufacturing-process knowledge, safety validation, and collaboration at real-world facilities. Cheaper computational discovery should enable more materials and applications to be explored, but physical testing, certification, capital investment, and production constraints will limit demand expansion. Because AI strongly assists the cognitive portions without fully reshaping the occupation's experimentally grounded core, the occupation remains resilient.

title: Mathematicians and statisticians
rationale: The occupation is almost entirely digital and cognitive, and AI can already accelerate coding, data cleaning, model selection, visualization, interpretation, and report drafting. Human expertise remains important for framing questions, designing valid studies, detecting methodological errors, and defending conclusions in scientific or regulated settings. Lower costs will unlock more analysis across business, healthcare, research, and government, but demand is constrained by available data, research budgets, regulation, and the number of consequential decisions requiring formal statistical work. Thus, substantial productivity gains will reshape skills and reduce some routine analytical roles, while preserving demand for statisticians who provide domain expertise, validation, and oversight.

title: Mechanical engineering technologists and technicians
rationale: AI-assisted CAD, simulation, specification review, test-data analysis, cost estimation, and technical reporting will materially accelerate the occupation's digital tasks. However, assembling prototypes, setting up physical tests, operating machinery, taking precise measurements, and troubleshooting equipment in factories still require hands-on presence and real-world judgment. Lower development costs should encourage more design iterations and some additional product development, but demand remains constrained by manufacturing investment and the number of physical systems being built. Because AI significantly improves the knowledge-work component without taking over the occupation's physical core, the occupation is resilient rather than highly disrupted.

title: Mechanical engineers
rationale: AI-enabled generative design, simulation, optimization, failure analysis, and technical documentation will materially transform the computer-intensive portions of mechanical engineering. Physical prototyping, testing, manufacturing integration, site investigation, safety validation, and professional accountability will continue to require substantial human judgment and real-world involvement. Lower engineering costs should unlock more product development, automation, and customized equipment, but capital costs, certification requirements, and manufacturing constraints limit demand expansion. The occupation therefore fits restructure: engineers will remain necessary, but their work will shift toward specifying problems, validating AI-generated designs, integrating systems, and overseeing physical execution.

title: Medical and health services managers
rationale: AI will materially automate scheduling, budgeting, billing oversight, compliance monitoring, record analysis, and report preparation. However, leadership, personnel management, regulatory accountability, stakeholder negotiation, and responses to clinical or operational emergencies still require human judgment and organizational presence. Healthcare growth and increasing administrative complexity will absorb some productivity gains, although demand for managers remains tied to facilities, staffing levels, and organizational structure. The occupation is therefore resilient because AI substantially improves its administrative components without fully reshaping its human-centered managerial core.

title: Medical assistants
rationale: AI can automate or accelerate scheduling, insurance paperwork, documentation, coding, inventory management, and parts of patient interviewing. However, core clinical duties such as taking vital signs, collecting specimens, giving injections, preparing examination rooms, and assisting patients require physical presence and interpersonal judgment. Lower administrative costs and an aging population may expand healthcare utilization, although provider capacity, regulation, and reimbursement limit the response. Because AI mainly changes the administrative portion rather than the occupation’s hands-on clinical core, medical assistants are resilient overall.

title: Medical dosimetrists
rationale: Most treatment planning, image review, dose calculation, optimization, and documentation are digital tasks that AI and automated planning systems can substantially accelerate. Human dosimetrists will remain important for unusual cases, quality assurance, regulatory accountability, equipment checks, and coordination with the oncology team, but these functions may require fewer labor hours per patient. Demand is constrained mainly by cancer incidence, physician prescriptions, treatment capacity, and clinical protocols, so cheaper planning will not produce a proportional increase in radiation treatments. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount pressure and a replace outcome.

title: Medical equipment repairers
rationale: The occupation is dominated by hands-on installation, calibration, disassembly, parts replacement, and testing at healthcare sites, all of which require dexterity and physical presence. AI can improve fault diagnosis, retrieve technical guidance, predict maintenance needs, and automate records, but it cannot readily perform the physical repair or assume responsibility for safety-critical equipment. Demand is relatively inelastic because maintenance volume is tied to the installed equipment base, regulatory schedules, and actual failures rather than the price of technician time. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI mainly enhancing technician productivity rather than replacing the core role.

title: Medical records specialists
rationale: The occupation is almost entirely computer-based and centers on extracting, validating, classifying, and entering structured information—tasks increasingly handled by AI-enabled EHR, coding, and document-processing systems. Humans will remain important for ambiguous documentation, provider clarification, audits, privacy compliance, and exception handling, but automation can substantially reduce routine coding and recordkeeping labor. Demand is driven mainly by the number of healthcare encounters and regulatory requirements, so making records processing much cheaper will not generate proportionately more work, although population aging will increase baseline volume.
