Human expertise remains important for eliciting undocumented knowledge, validating technical accuracy, understanding user needs, conducting usability work, and managing legal or safety risks. Lower costs will support more frequent updates, broader product coverage, and better documentation for smaller organizations, but demand remains constrained by the number of products, compliance needs, and users' limited appetite for documentation. The occupation therefore will restructure around subject-matter judgment, verification, information architecture, and AI-enabled content operations, with fewer roles focused mainly on drafting.

title: Telecommunications technicians
rationale: Core tasks involve traveling to worksites, climbing, handling cables and equipment, splicing fiber, and performing repairs in varied physical environments, which AI alone cannot readily execute. AI-enabled monitoring, diagnostics, scheduling, documentation, and troubleshooting guidance will improve productivity and reduce some remote or routine maintenance work. Cheaper service could support additional network upgrades and broader connectivity, but demand is constrained by infrastructure buildout cycles, capital budgets, and the declining maintenance needs of newer equipment. Because disruption remains low and concentrated in peripheral cognitive tasks, the occupation is resilient despite some ongoing employment pressure.

title: Tellers
rationale: Most teller transactions are routine, rules-based, and already being shifted to mobile banking, enhanced ATMs, video kiosks, and AI-enabled customer-service systems, although some cash handling and complex in-person interactions remain. Demand is highly inelastic because cheaper transaction processing will not cause customers to make substantially more deposits, withdrawals, or branch visits. High disruption combined with minimal demand expansion means banks can serve customers with fewer tellers, making replace the appropriate category.

title: Top executives
rationale: AI will materially automate executives’ analysis, reporting, planning, scheduling, drafting, and performance-monitoring tasks, although leadership, negotiation, accountability, and stakeholder trust remain human-intensive. Demand is relatively inelastic because organizations generally will not employ many more executives simply because managerial analysis becomes cheaper; instead, executives may oversee broader spans of activity with fewer supporting management layers. With disruption reaching the high threshold and elasticity remaining low, the aggregate occupation—especially general and operations managers—is likely to experience headcount pressure even though human chief executives remain necessary.

title: Tour and travel guides
rationale: AI can substantially assist with research, itinerary design, reservations, marketing, translation, and scripted narration, while apps and augmented-reality systems may substitute for basic informational tours. However, escorting groups, managing logistics and safety, adapting to real-world conditions, and providing engaging human interaction still require physical presence and interpersonal judgment. Lower-cost guidance may increase personalized and multilingual tour consumption somewhat, but demand is constrained by tourism volumes, site capacity, and travelers’ time, so the occupation remains resilient while its administrative and informational tasks become more automated.

title: Training and development managers
rationale: AI can substantially accelerate needs analysis, curriculum design, content creation, personalization, vendor evaluation, and measurement of training outcomes. However, stakeholder alignment, budget ownership, staff leadership, organizational judgment, and change management remain human-intensive. Lower costs and rapid workforce reskilling needs should expand training activity, but managerial demand is constrained by organizational budgets and spans of control. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-enabled learning strategy and oversight rather than experience wholesale replacement.

title: Training and development specialists
rationale: AI can already accelerate needs analysis, course design, content generation, assessment creation, program evaluation, and training administration, placing most of the occupation’s digital and cognitive tasks in its direct path. Human facilitation, organizational judgment, stakeholder coordination, and adaptation to workplace dynamics remain important, preventing near-total automation. Lower costs will support more customized and continuous training, especially as AI itself creates widespread reskilling needs, but employee time, compliance requirements, and corporate budgets limit how much training organizations will consume. The occupation therefore is likely to persist with substantially changed skills and higher output per specialist, fitting restructure.

title: Transportation, storage, and distribution managers
rationale: AI will materially automate routing, inventory planning, scheduling, compliance review, forecasting, reporting, and operational monitoring. However, managers will remain necessary for leadership, labor relations, safety accountability, facility oversight, cross-functional negotiation, and resolving unpredictable physical-world disruptions. Cheaper management and optimization can support growing e-commerce volumes and more complex supply chains, but demand is constrained by the underlying flow of goods and AI may let each manager oversee larger operations. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-assisted decision-making and exception management rather than experience either wholesale replacement or proportional job growth.

title: Travel agents
rationale: Nearly all core tasks—researching options, comparing fares, designing itineraries, explaining requirements, booking reservations, and handling changes—are digital and increasingly executable by AI connected to reservation systems. Human agents retain advantages in sales, accountability, complex disruptions, group travel, and luxury or specialized trips, but these represent a narrower share of the market. Cheaper planning may increase itinerary customization and make advisory services accessible to more travelers, yet travel demand remains constrained by consumers’ money and time, so it will not rise proportionally with productivity. High disruption combined with low demand elasticity therefore points to significant headcount contraction and concentration in complex, high-touch niches.

title: Tutors
rationale: Tutoring is predominantly cognitive and language-based, and current AI systems can already explain concepts, generate practice materials, provide feedback, and track progress. Human tutors retain advantages in motivation, trust, behavioral management, and adapting to subtle emotional or special-education needs, so disruption is very high rather than complete. Demand is highly elastic because personalized instruction has historically been constrained by cost and access, and cheaper tutoring could greatly increase its use across subjects, ages, and income groups. The result is augmentation: tutors who combine AI-generated instruction with human coaching can serve many more students, although routine homework help and test practice will face substantial automation.

title: Umpires, referees, and other sports officials
rationale: Computer vision, sensor systems, and automated replay will increasingly assist or replace specific calls such as line judgments, scoring, and ball tracking. However, the core role still requires real-world presence, dynamic positioning, safety oversight, contextual judgment, communication, and dispute management, especially in youth and amateur sports where advanced technology is less economical. Demand is tied mainly to the number of organized competitions, so cheaper officiating could support some additional events but is constrained by participation, facilities, schedules, and league funding. Because AI will significantly alter selected decisions without broadly eliminating the human-centered officiating role, the occupation is resilient overall.

title: Urban and regional planners
rationale: AI can materially accelerate GIS analysis, regulatory research, scenario modeling, site-plan review, report drafting, and public-presentation preparation, affecting a large share of planners’ knowledge work. However, field observation, stakeholder negotiation, public meetings, political judgment, and accountable approval recommendations remain human-centered. Lower costs could enable more frequent plan updates, deeper scenario analysis, and planning services for smaller jurisdictions, but government budgets, statutory processes, and finite development activity limit demand expansion. The occupation therefore is likely to restructure around AI-enabled analysis and stronger facilitation and judgment skills rather than disappear or expand proportionally with productivity.

title: Veterinarians
rationale: AI will materially assist with diagnostic reasoning, image interpretation, medical records, treatment planning, and owner communication. However, physical examinations, surgery, procedures, animal handling, emergency care, and emotionally sensitive interactions still require licensed veterinarians on site. Lower costs and faster service could unlock meaningful demand from budget-constrained pet owners and expand preventive care, although animal populations, owner willingness to pay, and clinic capacity limit that expansion. Because AI changes the cognitive portions of the job without replacing its hands-on core, the occupation is resilient.

title: Veterinary assistants and laboratory animal caretakers
rationale: Core tasks involve hands-on animal handling, cleaning, restraint, medication, sample collection, and perioperative care in unpredictable physical settings, placing most work beyond near-term AI capabilities. AI can improve scheduling, documentation, monitoring, and procedural guidance, while specialized robotics may automate some feeding or cleaning in laboratories, but these are peripheral or limited applications. Lower costs could moderately increase veterinary utilization and research capacity, although demand remains constrained by veterinarian availability, facility capacity, and research requirements. Because disruption to the core physical work is low, the occupation is resilient.

title: Veterinary technologists and technicians
rationale: Most core tasks require hands-on work with unpredictable animals, including restraint, specimen collection, anesthesia monitoring, imaging, nursing care, and treatment administration. AI can improve documentation, triage, diagnostic interpretation, patient monitoring, and owner communications, but it cannot readily replace physical presence, dexterity, or compassionate interaction. Lower costs could moderately expand veterinary care because some owners defer treatment for financial reasons, although veterinarian-supervision rules, pet populations, and household budgets limit expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient, with AI primarily improving peripheral cognitive and administrative tasks rather than reshaping the hands-on core.

title: Waiters and waitresses
rationale: AI-enabled kiosks, mobile ordering, automated payments, and scheduling tools can absorb order-taking and administrative tasks, but serving still centers on physical movement, real-time customer care, and handling unpredictable dining-room situations. Cheaper service may modestly increase restaurant demand, but meal frequency, venue capacity, and consumer preferences limit expansion. Because AI changes only part of the job while most core duties require human presence, the occupation is resilient, although staffing per restaurant may gradually decline.

title: Water and wastewater treatment plant and system operators
rationale: AI and advanced control systems can automate routine monitoring, optimize chemical dosing, detect anomalies, predict equipment failures, and streamline regulatory reporting. However, operators must still collect samples, inspect and maintain physical equipment, manage hazardous conditions, and respond on-site to malfunctions and emergencies. Demand is highly inelastic because treatment volumes are determined mainly by population, infrastructure, and regulation, so productivity gains will reduce staffing needs more than expand output. The occupation is resilient because its core retains substantial physical, safety-critical, and licensed human responsibilities, even though automation is likely to continue producing gradual headcount decline.

title: Water transportation workers
rationale: AI-enabled navigation, collision avoidance, route optimization, predictive maintenance, and automated recordkeeping will materially assist captains, officers, and engineers, with greater potential for reduced crewing on standardized routes. However, physical maintenance, passenger assistance, emergency response, local piloting, regulatory accountability, and operation in unpredictable marine conditions still require onboard personnel. Demand is relatively inelastic because shipping labor is only one component of transport costs and cargo volumes are driven mainly by trade and commodity demand, so cheaper operation would not generate proportionally more voyages. With disruption remaining moderate over the next decade, the occupation is resilient overall, although some routine watchkeeping roles may decline.

title: Web developers and digital designers
rationale: Nearly all core tasks—coding, interface design, prototyping, testing, content integration, and performance analysis—are digital and increasingly supported or automated by generative AI. Human judgment remains important for translating client needs, managing complex integrations, ensuring usability, and validating output, but workflows and required skills will change substantially. Demand is highly elastic because lower development costs enable more businesses and individuals to build, customize, and continuously improve websites and digital interfaces. This expanding market should absorb much of the productivity gain, making augmentation more likely than broad occupational replacement, although routine entry-level work will face pressure.

title: Welders, cutters, solderers, and brazers
rationale: Core welding and cutting tasks require manual dexterity, physical positioning, safety judgment, and adaptation to varied materials and job-site conditions. AI-enabled vision, robotic welding, blueprint interpretation, and automated quality inspection will affect repetitive manufacturing work, but many repair, construction, and custom-fabrication tasks remain difficult to automate. Cheaper and faster welding could modestly expand fabrication and infrastructure output, although demand is constrained by broader construction and manufacturing activity, material costs, and capital budgets. With disruption remaining low, the occupation is resilient overall, despite automation pressure in standardized factory settings.

title: Wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives
rationale: AI can automate prospect identification, personalized outreach, product recommendations, quotations, order processing, CRM updates, reporting, and routine customer support, materially reducing the labor required per account. Complex negotiations, technical consultations, trade shows, site visits, and relationship building remain human-intensive, preventing an even higher disruption score. Demand for sales coverage may expand among smaller accounts, but it is constrained by the underlying volume of goods sold and customers’ limited appetite for additional sales contact. Consequently, productivity gains are likely to reduce representative headcount, especially in inside sales and standardized product categories, while preserving more technical and relationship-driven roles.

title: Wind turbine technicians
rationale: AI can improve remote monitoring, predictive maintenance, fault diagnosis, scheduling, and service documentation. However, the occupation’s core tasks require technicians to travel to turbines, climb towers, inspect equipment, and physically repair complex electrical, mechanical, and hydraulic systems in hazardous environments. Demand can expand as lower maintenance costs support additional wind deployment, although it remains constrained by the number of installed turbines and their service needs. Because AI primarily assists diagnosis and administration rather than replacing hands-on fieldwork, the occupation is resilient.

title: Woodworkers
rationale: Most core tasks involve physically handling materials, setting up and monitoring machinery, assembling products, finishing surfaces, and making real-world quality and safety judgments. AI can improve design interpretation, CNC programming, inspection, maintenance, and production planning, but broader displacement would require capable robotics and greater factory automation rather than software AI alone. Cheaper production could increase demand for customized furniture, cabinetry, and renovation products, although durable-goods demand and construction activity impose limits, so the occupation remains resilient despite gradual automation.

title: Writers and authors
rationale: Writing is almost entirely digital and language-based, and generative AI already materially accelerates research, ideation, drafting, rewriting, and adaptation across formats. Lower production costs will unlock substantially more personalized marketing, online publishing, self-publishing, and multimedia content, although finite audience attention and demand for trusted human voices limit elasticity. Because output demand should expand significantly while human judgment, originality, source development, and reputational accountability remain valuable, the occupation is likely to be augmented and substantially reshaped rather than broadly eliminated.

title: Zoologists and wildlife biologists
rationale: AI will substantially accelerate species identification, camera and acoustic monitoring, GIS analysis, population modeling, literature review, and report writing. However, field observation, specimen collection, animal handling, experimental design, and context-sensitive conservation decisions still require substantial human presence and expertise. Cheaper analysis and monitoring could expand ecological research across more species and habitats, but government funding constraints and limited conservation budgets cap that expansion. The occupation is therefore resilient overall, although its analytical workflows will become significantly more AI-enabled.
